3.7actru. FAIR SUMMER. Tastes differ we are often told, Yet he who well and wisely reasons Must surely thee, fair Summer, hold To be the queen of all the seasons. ,The charm of Spring we would not scorn, But Spring's a maiden coy and fickle; Awl Autumn lays thy golden corn Too soon beneath his eager sickle. Theformer seems, compared with thee, A compound of east wind and tillage;• The latter, jocund though he be, Is far too fond of spoil and pillage. So while thy rule is firm as now, Bet ore a ruthless hand he raises To pluck the roses from thy brow, Fair Summer, let me sing thy praises. Each day brings laughter and delight, —1 New health, to sickness balm to sorrow; And the soft beauty of the night But ushers in a sweeter morrow. . • r. The birds' glad hymns are never done, The very bees with joy are humming; What wonder, handmaid of the sun. Our hearts make merry at thy corning. —"Leisure Hour" for JttlY

THE BRAIN.— brain by idleness as by overwork. Intellectual power is lessened by the listlessness in which some persons spend their lives. Under such conditions the brain gradually loses its health, and although equal to the demands of a routine existence is unable to withstand the strain of sudden emergency. So when a load of work is unex- pectedly thrown on it in its unprepared state, the worst consequences of what may be called overwork show themselves. Similarly a man accustomed to sedentary pursuits is liable to he physically injured by taking sud- denly to violent exercise. A certain gentleman from the North, being of a genealogical turn of mind, believed that he discovered in his pedigree some remote connection with the Royal Stuart blood. Going South, he made much ot the pre- sumed relationship, until he was generally spoken of, in bated breath, by his innocent English friends, as." A descendant of the Stuarts." At a large public gathering he was thus mentioned, and the description instantly engaged the rapt interest of a stranger, a new arrival from Caledonia. "A deseendanto' the Stuarts l" he cried. "Eh, sirs, I'd like fine to see ane o' the auld Royal race !" "Then there he is," answered his interlocutor, pointing him out—"there—the gentleman standing in front of the fire-place." " Gude sakes !" cried the astonished Scot; "that's just my am n bnther Jock !" A lady went into one of our fashionable shops recently to buy a wrap, and, in course of hersearch for the right thing, picked up from the countei, a cloth jacket, the colour of which greatly pleased her. It was dark red, but heavily braided, and to her taste it would have looked better without the elaborate trimming. Holding it up to inspect its peculiar cut, she said to the attendant, "I should like this one. It is very handsome, except for all that common passementerie on the front." "Excuse me, madame," said a voice behind her, in haughty tones, "excuse me, that is my jacket, which I have just laid off, to try on another !" The lady, who is keenly alive to situations, says she felt like "One-of the things better left unsaid," in Punch, and got out of the way as quickly as possible. OSIRIS UNVEILED.—There is quite a large class of men whose repugnance to moral restraint makes them detest Christianity, yet who have intellect enough to compel them to think and just enough conscience to make them uneasy when they have no formal belief in the super- natural. Such men generally become enthusiastic over some "creed outworn" of the ancients. The more vague it is morally the better they like it. Once they wildly adored Buddha, for he not only founded a faith but abandoned his wife; their enthusiasm cooled, however, when investigation developed that Buddha detested sel- fishness, and, that, although he had left his own wife, he never established irregular relations with the wife of any other man. Then, in an idotic, intense way, they went over to Brahma and Nirvana, because the former had been idealised as somebody who looked wise but said nothing, while Nirvana was an unutterable nothinge ness that had no equal except the used-up mind of the modern man who tried to believe in it. But scholarship, which takes a fiendish delight in upsetting antiquated beliefs, discovered that Brahma was a creation of priestcraft, so the ',earners after a creed that would let them be senti- mental without compelling them to be virtuous sped away to the Nile and vowed allegiance to Isis and Osiris; for these deities, although of good reputation, did not leave behind them an exasperating lot of moral injunctions to make life miserable for their followers. But now Osiris is under a cloud; the Egyptian religious records found in a recently Opened pyramid are said to give the coup de grace to Osiris. What are the godless worshippers to do flow? Jove will not answer their purpose, for, although he occasionally got drunk and sometimes gave Juno justification for divorce suits, there was a sturdy straightforwardness, about him that is very distasteful to people to whom nothing is adorable unless vague. Their only chance is to transfer their devotions to the devil, fcir he, besides becoming some- what misty under textual investigation and clerical con- cession, is ideally in sympathy with their tastes, and detests moral restraint and all other morality as heartily as they themselves do. coca. "And," said Father Malone, gazing fearlessly around upon the crowd, many of whom looked anything but friendly—though no one would have dared .to lay hands on him—" if. there's anyone here—an' I know there's more than one--as would follow in Patrick Doolan's steps, I tell them here an' how that they'll do a wicked deed before God an' man, an' if they meet Doolan's fate 'twill sarye 'em roight." At this juncture there witi a stir in the crowd with- out, and two constables made their way into the cot- tage. They had come to remove the body to the inn at Ballygoyle, there to await an inquest, and to take possession of the rifle with which Doolan had fired at Mr. Lorraine. It was well Father Malone was preSent, or the excited and ignorant people would probably have opposed the constables; but the priest enforced order, and ,the people quietly allowed, the police to do their duty. This done, one of the constables pro- ceeded to Curramore, and informed Vincent Lorraine that he would be required to attend the inquest on the following day, to give evidence. Lorraine was talking to his agent, Dan Murphy, when the constable Caine, and when that functionary had departed the young man turned to Murphy, and said— • "The inquest takes, place' to-morrow; the day after Dermot Grady haa his notice.. Be his child well or ill, he will, turn out of his farm • no remonstrance, :Murphy. I serve the notice with' my own hand. I don't want you tor be murdered; I would far rather you left the place." , "No, yeeanner, no, I'll not do that; I'll stand by ye. They've noVthritened me since yer Inner took matthers into yer own hand; but I'd rather ye let me sarve the notice."' "NO, Murphy. You know I never go back from what I say. Regan's rent is due in two days. I have had a warning that if I demand it it will be the worse for me. If Regan, does net pay he will have his notice." "But, sorr, ye know .the bhoys 'll put the tinants back again." "They had best get some canvas then and pitch tents," returned Lorraine, taking out a cigar, "for they shall have no roof to cover them. If I burn down every cottage on the estate, Dan Murphy, I will be master. My tenants can submit or starve.. They call me cruel, and perhaps you think I am, but I am not. Yet I tell you that if one of these men, starving through his own crime and folly, begged bread of me, I Would not give it. They bring famine on themselves, and then stretch out their hands to England for food. They are not ashamed to beg of the men whose blood, even while they eat the bread of their charity, they shed and call it a righteous deed." "Aye, sorr," said Murphy, sorrowfully, "'tis too thrue what ye say, and 'tis many the tohne swate Miss Hyacinth has said the same; the disgrace makes her heart so sore." .

The Mayor (Alderman Pi cktnere) presided, and there were also present Aldermen Hololes, Webster, Davies, Sut- ton, H Arrison ; Councillors Greening, Dixon, Taylor, Marsh, W. Pierpoint, ',Tinsley. Platt, Mackie, Jolley, Hutchinson, Tinsley, F. A, Roberts, Bolton; Brook (town clerk), Whittle (deputy town clerk), and Chor- ley (borough treasurer.) -

It was further resolved that the plan of "give and take" lines in Factory-lane, submitted by Mr. John White, be agreed to. Councillor PLATT, in moving the adoption of the minutes, said that the offer of a "give and take line "in Factory- laae, which had been submitted by Mr. John White on be. half of Lord Winmarleigh, was considered very satisfactory by the committee, and when carried out would be a great improvement to Factory-lane. • Al,'ertnan SPY] ON seconded the resolution, which was agreed to without discussion. SANITARY COMMITTER—THE INTERCEPTING DEPOT '

If Dan Murphy was " speering,” as a Scotchman would have said, he gained nothing, for Lorraine's face was inscrutable; he made a careless rejoinder, and pre- sently the agent bowed himself out, and Lorraine hummed softly to himself--

But Tracy Mansfield hummed no love song as he strode over the common in the long rays of the wester- ing sun. Vincent Lorraine's words last night were still burning in his soul, and the Englishman's haughty security in his own position and utter contempt for his rival, drove the young Irishman nearly to madness. When he reached the Wood Cottage he found Mrs. Desmond alone. Hyacinth was out—had not gone far, her mother said, and would be in soon. "It is Hyacinth you want to see, of course," she said, quietly, and Tracy answered frankly, "Yes. I can bear suspense no longer after last night, and what that villain said----"

" Lorraine?" interrupted Mrs. Desmond. "Did you speak to him, Tracy?" "Aye, how could I help it? How could any man who loved a woman see another man—and a profligate like Lorraine—doing his best to break her heart ?" , "Tell me, Tracy, what passed between you and Vincent Lorraine."

And Mansfield obeyed. Mrs. Desmond listened in silence. Then she said— " You were wrong, Tray. Hyacinth is not engaged to you; and you had no right to assume that Vincent Lorraine meant nothing but trifling. You know how .1 feel with regard to him, and if even Hyacinth were ' attracted by him she would not oppose me; and I do not, see how Mr. Lorraine, whatever he may -say, can ,exactly dispense with my consent. That consent he ,will never have. You acted in a hot-headed manner, Tracy, and lam sorry you did so. You may speak to Hyacinth, but I cannot give you much hope; she may be able to do so. Hash here she comes."

At a mer tinz of the Sanitary Committee it was resolved "that the tender of Mr Isaac Ashcroft, of Orford, for the purchase of the manure from the Corporation stables, for the next twelve ,months, at 5s ed per ton, be ac- cepted." Alderman SUTTON moved, and Councillor GREENING seconded, the adoption of the minutes. Councillor DIXON said be understood an accident had occurred at the works at Longford, and he should like to have some information about it, as there was nothing in the minutes about it. Councillor PLATT said the chairman of the committee was not present, or be should have called his attention to the fact that there was no implovement whatever of the nuisance at the intercepting depot. Pe could not help ex- pressing the opinion that he thought the intercepting depots a gigantic mistake, and he was sure that if any private firm created such a nuisance the Sanitary Committee would take very prompt steps. (Hear, hear.) Alderman SUTTON replied that the committee were doing all they possibly could to abate the nuisance, and he was not aware of anything of great moment occurring at the present time. He bad no doubt that if per ple would have a little bit of patience till things got into fair working order they would have very little to complain about. With regard to Courmillo% Dixon's quertion, there bad been an accident at the depot,lut it was of a slight character. It might have been worse.and the coot f it would si nply be a few pounds. It was only a slight accident, such a one as would occur where machinery was used, The raion.es were thin adopted.

At a meeting held on the 14th July the Bathkeeper ported that the income from the baths f.rr the past four weeks was £6O 9a, and for the corresponding period last year £35 10s 101. It was resolved "That six or steven-ef the pillars and chains. be removed from' the west' drive to the +met drive in front of the Town Hall,". and "Tbat the wall in front of the Town Hail be removed, and that the plan now submitted, No.l, showing the taking dowa of the wall between the skrubberies, fora distance of about 45 yards, to within 2 feet 6 inches. from the level of ground. The wall to have a new stone coping, surmounted by an iron rail- ing ; estimated cost, £150." , The MAYOR, referring to the Minute regarding the wall, said the ' committee had not vet quite decided what the character of the alterations should be. They had, there- . fere, thought it advisable, on further consideration, to with- draw the resolution so thatemmething more tasty and orna- mental could be suggested. He moved that the minutes be confirmed with the exception of the one referring to the 'Wall in front of the Town Hall. • (Hear, bean) Alderman HARRISON seconded' the propotitiou, and said there was no difference of opinion, as to the desirability of making an 'alteration; the. maly difference was as to whether they should not sPend is little more money than £l5O. (Hear, hear.) AlthOugh" he assented at once to the withdrawal of the resolution foe the substitution of one which would give the committee more ample powers, as far as be was con- cerned he should have been very 'well pleased even to have had the work done for £l5O, because. even that scheme would have been immensely suoerier to 'the present appear. ance of the front of that handsome buildiug. • (Hear, hear.) Councillor PLATT said that on the committee he opposed the adoption of the resolution, and one reason why he did so was that he thought the removal of tne wall—though he dared say he was very much in a minority—could very well wait until the rates were less. (Hear, hear.) He was prepared be see the wall stand for a year or two. ouncillor GREENING endorsed the remarks of Mr. Platt. If the work was to be done at all they ought to do it pro- perly. His °Melia was that the wall was best as it is and should be left alone. Aldermen HOLMES pointed out that the estimates for the whole of the year had been passed by the Council, but there was no estimate for any expenditure upon the Town Hall wall. A lderman SUTTON supposed that when this matter came up again for discussion they would have two schemes laid before them—an alternative scheme beside the one referred to in the minutes If there were two schemes they could adopt one at £l5O or more. It was quite necessary the wall should he pulled down—(hear, hear. and "No, no,")—and considering that Sir Gilbert Greenall had promised an ex- pensive fountain the wall ought certainly to be removed. 'The place looked more like a prison than anything else. He wee rather afraid there was something more in the matter than the cost. COUTICIiiUr HUTCHINSON said he trusted the Committee would bring out another scheme. it was very desirable that the wall should be removed even if it cost a little more . money. Its removal would be a great boon to the town, and particularly to the-people parading Sankey St. on Sat- urday and Sunday. (Hear, hear.) The resolution was then carried. GAS COMMITTEE.—THE AUDIT. At a meeting of this committee, on the 22nd July, the average illuminating power of the gas for the past four weeks was reported to be equal to 18 candles at both works. The following letter was read :—" 83, Golborne-street, War- rington, 6th July, 1887. The Chairman of the Gas Works Committee, Warrington. Dear Sir,—l have the pleasure to report having completed my audit of books and accounts of the gas department for the two half years ended 25th March last, as instructed, which I have found correct and satisfac- tory in every respect. I have followed throughout the usual couree as heretofore, comparing the cash book entries with cash receipt foils, paid accounts, bank book, respectively. All additions have been carefully gone over, and the summaries checked against the respective ledger accounts, thence to profit and loss and balance state- ment, which has already been before you. The revenue ac- count and balance sheet have been verified and certified in ledger and in report for publication. In conclusion, I must add that the accounts are thoroughly and efficiently kept, and have to render my acknowledgments to Mr Paterson. Mr Cooper, and assistants for their uniform kindness in afford- ing every facility for proper examination.—Yours respect- fully, B. K. Alderman 'lemmas, in moving the confirmation of the minutes, said it must be gratifying to the members of the Council to Bee the report which had been presented by Mr B Kendrick. he might state that it was decided by the Council a few months ago, that the borough auditors should also exambre the Gels C immittee'e accounts. They had not yet completed that work—they had not a couple of days ago at any rate—but they had devoted a great deal of time anti attention to the work. He could not anticipate their report, but he believed it would be very satisfactory as far as it went. (Hear, hear.) Alderman WEBSTER seconded the. raotien,-which was carried.

UNFOUNDED CHARGES AGAINST MIL DILLON.— A SCENE. •

M. Diereow rose excitedly to call ' attention to eentain statements made about himself in a Mayo newspaper, which be described as of a disgusting and offensive.charecter, and which be alleged had emanated from certain Conservative gentlemen below the Ministerial gangway. The expressions objected to occurred in a description of the conduct of cer- tain.lrish members, especially Mr. Dillon himself, during the reading of an answer to a question referring to an attack upon come Protestant school ceildren in Mayo d trine their return from a picnic, in the course of which the daughter of the agent of the Marquis of Sligo had been eeriously injured in the face with a stone. Tee newspaper report described Mr. Dillon and his colleagues as receiving the ac- count of the attack on the children and 'the injury to ' the young lady with cheers and laughter. .While Mr. Dillon was reading the newspaper account to the House several members from below the Conservative gangway shouted out "True" when he came to the message describ- ing the laughter. Imagining that the cry of "True" came from the Solicitor-General, he immediately, with increasing excitement, challenged the honourable and learned gentle- man with having used the expression. Sir Edward Clarke at once rose and denied the charge. Mr. Halsey, Mr. R G. Webster, Mr. J. W. Mel.ean, and Captain Price darted to their feet, and asserted that they had heard the laughter on the occasion in question. '• I say it is false," shouted Mr. Dillon, in a state of furious excitement; and he proceeded to charge scum of the members who had risen with heviog supplied the account to the 51amo paper. lie declared it to be an infamous and atrocious falsehood, and if he was to be bounded out of public life in this country, he for one would not stand it. For some time the Speaker had been trying to arrest the voluble flew of Mr. Dillon's indignation by cries of "Order, order ;" and Mr. Dillon only resumed his seat when the ' Speaker's voice had risen, 'to its full pitch, tied when Mr. Dillon's own words were drowned in the general cry of " Order," which came from the Ministerial benches: The Speaker in- formed Mr Dillon that he must not make charges of that kind against honourable members, to which Mr Dillon an- grily replied that while he was II the very act of repudiat- ing the charge in the newspaper, four members had got up and maintained that the statement was true. lie claimed the protection of the House. and informed the Speaker that he had often heard him cell members to order for language which sank into ineignificance besides this. The Speaker rose, and with marked emphasis said," I am the judge of order." After which he preceded to put a conciliatory in- terpretation on the interruptiou of the four Conservative members. " I demand to be heard," exclaimed Mr McLean. " Surely we have a right to speak when these monstrous accusations are made against us." Again the Speaker shouted "Order," and said that if any honourable member wished to make an explanation he was entitled to do so. Mr Dillon then resumed his mat, and Mr McLean, after again referring with vehement indignation to Mr Dillon's charges. stated that he had distinctly heard the laughter of the Irish members when it was mentioned a week ago that a young lady had emir struck in the face with a stone ; but, as Mr Dillon denied th-et he had joined in the lauehter, he ef course acquitted the honourabie member. Mr Webeter next made an almost ineffecmel effort to be heard in cor- roboration of Mr McLean. Mr Dillon, however, persisted in asserting that some Conservatives had contradicted him when he denied the newspaper charge. The Speaker closed the incident with the conciliatory remark that he had settled the point of order, and, he believed, settled it to the satisfaction of the House THE IRISH LAND BILL THE IEIBII LAND BILL-BANKRUPTCY CLAUSES DROPPED. ELECTION NEWS.

NORTII-WEST WILTS. At a meeting of Liberal delegates at Chippenhern en Saturday, Mr. John. Fuller, eldest son of Mr. J. P. Fuller, M.P. for West Wilts, was unanimously selected as Liberal candidate for North-West Wilts. Mr. Fuller had written that he was a strong follower' of Mr. Gladstone, and would accept the invitation. FOREST OF DEAN.—RESULT OF POLL.

Owing to the wide area over which the nineteen poll- ing districts were scattered, the result of Frirday's polling in the contest for the representation of the Forest of Dean (Gloucestershire) Division, was not ascertainable until after one o'clock on Saturday, when the following official announcement was made :

SAMUELSON ((IL.) WYNDHAM (C.) Majority 1,550 1886.—Mr. T. Blake (L), 3,822; Mr. F. L. Lucas (U.L.), 2,415: majority, 1,407. 1885.—Blake (L.), 5,143; Punkett (C.), 2,421-2,722. When the result of the poll was declared at Nevrn- ham there were only a few hundred persons present No excitement was manifested, as a Liberal victory had been taken for granted. Mr. Samuelson, M.P., in return- ing thanks, said the result would have the same effect upon the Government as the other by-elections, as jt showed that on a heavier poll there was a larger Liberal majority. The electors were coming round to Mr. Glad- stone's views.
CUIIIIENT POLITICS.

At the annual meeting of the 'Peebles and Selkirk Liberal Association a letter was read from Sir C. Tennant expressing his conviction that the cause that the mem- bers of the association have at heart is gaining ground, and mentioning that he had seen Mr. Gladstone, who wal in the best of spirits. Lord Charles Beresford received, in the course of Friday, a letter from the Queen, declining to accept his resignation of the office of Lord of the Admiralty. The formal breach of etiquette is therefore condoned, and his lordship remains in office. It is stated that Sir John Pope Hennessy has instituted legal proceedings against The Times for libel, the damages being laid at £20,000. Tim alleged libel is cortained in an article which ap- peared in The Times some months back dealing with the action of Sir John in the Mauritius. Sir John returns to the Mauritius in October.

The Irish Times London correspondent says :—The contemplated Liberal plan of campaign during the recess will be on a grand scale. Nearly every competent speaker of the Liberal Opposition and the whole Nation- alist party will be engaged in the movement, which will be mainly confined to Great Britain. It is said that Mr. Gladstone and other Liberal leaders have been in con- ference with Mr. Parnell, and the ex-Premier is sanguitv. as to the result. The same correspondent states that Mr. O'Donnell is determined to persevere with his action against The Times, notwithstanding strong pressure from more than one influential quarter.

Writing to a Welsh correspondent on the question of the anti-tithe agitation in Wales, Mr. Chamberlain says lie gime his vote the other night against the adjourn- Ment of the House on the tithe riots question and the delay Whiph etch adjournment would have caused. The Welsh people, he says, are being deceived by their ad- visers, but he has no doubt that in the long run they will do him (Mr. ChaMberlain) justice. He disapproves of the resort to violence, as with the extension of the fran- chise the fullest opportunity is now given to all to secure redress by constitutional means. On Saturday, a Primrose League demonstration was held at Hutton Park, near Bolton. Special trains were run from all the neighbouring towns, and, the day being fine, there was a large concourse of people. There were three platforms, from which simultaneously were proposed three resolutions expressing confidence in the Govertp merit in their endeavour to maintain the union of Great Britain and 'lreland, and urging the promotion of the principles of the Primroge T.,eague. Among the speakers were. Colonel Bridgernan 'and- Mr. H. Shepherd Cross, 'members for Bolton; Mr. Lees Knos&lPs, member for Salford; the Hon. George Curzon, member for South- port; Mr. Frank Harelcastle, M.P., and Sir Frederick Milner. . . . _

Mr. Gladstone has received a communication from the lion. secretaries to a meeting of citizens of Brisbane con- vened by - the Mayor at the request of a number of influential citizens who sympathise with him and his party in opposition .to the Crimes Act. The communi- cation states that the Act was opposed vigorously by all sections ot the Colonists of Brisbane without distinction of class or creed, that the meeting was attended by many distinguished citizens, and that great enthusiasm prevailed. The sneakers included Mr. W. .Brooks, jun., member for Brisbane, !he Hon. P. Perkins, formerly Minister for Lands, the Hon. H. 13olion, formerly Post- master-General in the colony of Victoria, and the Hon. A. J. Thynna An open-air demonstration was held, under the auspices of the Home Rule Union, in Potter's Park, Man- chester, on Saturday, Several thousand people were present, and the speaking was conducted from two platforms. presided over by Mr. C. J. Fleming and Mr. J. A Picton, M.P. The principal speakers were Mr. Sexton, ALP., and Mr. Michael Davitt. At each of the meetings a resolution WAS passed •pr testing against the utterly i unjustifiable action of the Government n inflicting upon lteland a most vindictive and outrageous Coercion Bill. The resolution affirmed that the absence of any facts to justify exceptional legislation in Ireland formed additional evidence that the object of the Government in confiscating the moit ordinary rights and liberties of the Irish people was to place the tenants more than ever in the power of the landlords. Satisfaction was expressed at the union existing between the democracies of Great Britain and Ireland, which it was hoped would bring about a speedy reinolval of the infamous measure. In the evening Mr. Sexton was entertained to dinner at the Grand Hotel. In the course of his reply to the toast of the Irish Parliamentary party he stated that the party is in high heart, that the leader is fit for his work, that the prospect is propitious, and that the end is certain. Mr. Thomas Newbigging and Mr. 3, H. Crosfield replied to the toast of "Our English friends." ..

A private meeting of the Committee of Liberal county members Was held on Monday in one of the House of Commons committee-rooms to receive the report of the Sub-committeeeppointed tg draw amendments to the Government Altotments Bill. Sir •Bernhard Samuelson presided. The amendments agreed upon cover generally the following points :-1. The sanitary authority must put the Act in force on a representation by ten or more inhabitants, unless the representation on fuller inquiry is shown to be without foundation. 2. To buy land com- pulsorily the sanitary authority shall be eabled to act at once on a certificate of the Local Government Board, titter the usual locallngqiry, the procedure proposed in the bill involving considerable delay on account of the reference to county magistrate, the Local Governmeot Board, and finally to Parliament. 3. To carry out the mianagement of , allotments in conjunction with the fmnitary authority local committees shall be freely elected by Parliamentary electot4 and ratepayers in urban sani- tary districts and parishes on the principle of one man one vote. 4. The proposal that allotments shall be limited to one acre shall be amended by the adoption of Mr. Jesse Collings's proposal that allotments should be one acre of arable land or three acres of pasture. .

Lord Cross, speaking at Chard on Monday, said it was urged that because Lord Flartington gave advice to ths Government that they were always ready to receive; therefore Lord Salisbury should step aside and Lord flartington should take his place. But the moment Lord Hartington was in ofrsee it would be said "it was bad enough to have the Conservatives in power with 315 members, hut you have only some 80." He argued that the Government had laboured to restore to Ireland thet liberty which we enjoyed in this country, and it was their deliberate intention to make use of every one of, the powers which Parliament had entrusted to theist They were also determined to pass the Land Bill. ,True, they had made alterations so that more redress might be, Riven to the tenant. Thera was a third queztion which they honed to bring forward next year, by which the tenant might he enabled to purchase his land at a reason- able price. He could not avoid saying that the conduct of Mr. Gladstone had been such as to bring discredit and disgrace upon one who had been among the foremost statesmen of the age.

div.p: FUNI'RAL oF TAR 1-41 VIE MR, ROB ail
VERDIN, M.P.

The remains of the late Mr. Robert Verdin, M.P., were interred on Saturday afternoon at the Parish Church of Davenham. If anything were wanting to complete the expression of affection for the mem- ory of the deceased, it was found in the aspect of the immense concourse of spectators who gathered on the ,entle slope upon Which the beautiful church of Davenham rests. The-.time announced for the funeral to leave The Brockhurst was two o'clock, and long before that hour all' footsteps were turned in the direction of Davenham. By two o'clock most of those intending to take part in the mournful pro- ceedings had passed through the main entrance to the grounds. The extensive lawns surrounding The Brock h urst afforded ample space for the marshalling of the procession. On the lawn to the left of the house more than eight hundred porkmen stood four deep. They were bareheaded as the body was borne through their midst. Many of the men could not conceal their emotion which they in common with the town feel at the loss of a considerate employer and a kind friend. On the opposite lawn, the re- presentatives of public bodies and private com- panies took up their position. In the roadway were gathered hundreds of spectators whose silence as the body was carried through the gates gave the scene additional impressiveness and solemnity. Ex- tending down the road were numerous private car-, tinges, some closed, but the greater part being occu- pied by persons desirous of paying a last tribute of respect to the deceased. Two o'clock was passed when the first part of the procession left the B: rock- ' hurst. From the gates to Davenham Church, a distance of fully two miles, both sides of the road were lined with spectators who displayed the ut- most respect. The order of the procession was as follows :—Representatives of Davenham Constitu- tional Club, boys of Witton Grammar School, Wins- ford• Conservative Club, Winsford Liberal Club, Watermen's Friendly Society, Cheshire Lines and L. and N.- VV. Railway Go, Phtenix Park Salt Works Northwich Gas Company; Tradesmen, Residents, Sze., Gladstone Liberal Club, Davenham Liberal Club, Weston Point Pierhead Men, Northwich Vic- toria Football Club, Northwich Local Board, Wins- ford Local Board, Northwich Conservative Associa- tion. Then came the hearse and 13 mourning coaches, in which were seated the relatives of the deceased. Following were a large number of pri- vate carriages containing many well known public men. Amongst these were Messrs Milne, A. Malam, Reekie, Rogerson, Carter, Bradley, Barton, Nancol- lis, R Stubbs, W Stubbs, Joseph Burton, Darwell, sen , Darwell, jun., Thomas Rayner, James Rayner, Lee, Rev Mr Whitfield, J Mosley, Rutter, Leyland, Earlam, Moreland, Newton, John Thompson, Lovett, Buckley, Blewer. II J Thompson, F J Thompson, J J Dixon, L W Marsh, E Milner. T H Forgan, and (representinlg Messrs Brunner, Mond & Co) H E Falk, and Mr T Moor (president and secretary of the Salt Chamber of Commerce respectively) ; Mr James Newell, Rev C Spencer Stanhope, General Eaton, Surgeon-General Johnston, Rev Mr Moberley, W Beach, George Hamlett, Joseph Littler, Rev Pro- fessor Holliday, Major Skidmore, George Dutton, George Cliff, Hey Mr Laidman, T Handley, R Clark, W Handley (secretary, Runcorn Liberal Association), F J Norman, Philip Speakman, J J Speakman, Rev John Lockwood. The following clerks in the em- ploy of Messrs Joseph Verdin• and Sons, Liverpool, Winsford, and Runcorn, also followed in carriages: —Messrs T Whrlow, H Goodwin, C E Side, J Mills, G Millington, R Boyning,' W Brogden, S Sadler, G Robinson, W Hough, H Parry, II Fryer, II Parker, Davies,' and A E Musgrave. Besides the :private carriages of those whose names have already been mentioned were those of- Mrs Shackerly, Captain Turner. J P, Mr L Mond, and Mr J T Brunner.

Immediately behind the private carriages were the captains and hands of the river craft .of Messrs Joseph Verdin and Sons, several of the captains carrying handsome wreaths and crosses, Then came upwards of 800 employes of Messrs Joseph Verdin and Sons, and 60 members of tlie Victoria Lodge of Oddfellows, No. 186 Davenham. At Davenham the ranks were joined by the mem- bers of Northwich Board ot Guardians. Amongst those who met the body t Davenham Church were Mr. J. Brundrit, J.P., Mr. G. Lloyd Wigg, and Mr. F. A.Lake, of Runcorn. The officiating ministers were the Rev. W. H. France-Hayhurst, rector of Daven- ham, and the Rev. Mr. Butler, curate, and the ser- vice was of a most solemn description. Amongst the very numerous floral tributes placed in the vault with the coffin and on the grave were wreaths from Dr. McDougall and the Runcorn clerks. Dr. McDougall occupied a seat in the twelfth mourning coach.

He is largely interested in silver mining, and its more senses than one may be said to have "silver on the brain," for about the commencement of his successful career, he received a blow which free ured his skull, and was only saved from death by the operation of trepanning—that is to say, a plate of silver was inserted in the top of his head. He is still a young man, and thoull his halr is not "silvered." his skull is; thus differing from many men andfwomen, who have no silver on their brain, but a tare supply of it In their hair. The hair is a vegetable, and may be cultivated, its growth strength- ened, and its texture improved by mire, attention, and the application of the proper fertilizing ipropertlei.: That this is the case has been amply demonstrated, and :therefore no one need have thin or grey hair, or a coarse and wiry stubble, provided they will use the proper care. At the meeting of the British Medical ASSOCIAItiOII on Wednesday, a resolution was passed cdndemning the eystem of building houses b‘ck to back, snd calling for legislation to enforce a minimum amount of open space at the front and in the rear of all dwellings. Dr. Bridgewater, of Har- row, has been elected President of the Council of the Asso- ciation for the ensuing three years. BREAM OF PRODOSE.—A young man named flicturd Walter Stead, said to have an income of between £1,500 and £2OOO a year, was the defendant in an action for breach of promise of marriage heard at the Leeds Assizes on Wednesday. The plaintiff, a shop girl at Knaresborongh, had been basely wronged by the defendant, of whose con- duct the jury expressed their condemnation bt ordeiing him to pay £1,500 AO damages.

div.head: GLASGOW (BRIDGETON DIVISION).
div.p: GLASGOW (BRIDGETON DIVISION).

Sir George Trevelyan, addressing an open-air meeting at Glasgow on Saturday, referred with indignation to the attacks made on himself, and contrasted these with the statesmanlike speeches nt Mr. T. P. O'Connor and others on his behalf. He referred to the subject of local government, observing that while in Glasgow the local authority was the Town Council, in the country they had no -decent local government, and powers had to be entrusted to the Boards of Trade, who were elected on a ' property suffrage, or magistrates, whom he would keep to their proper work. The magistrates appointed by the Lords-Lieutenant were selected from one class and usually from one creed in Ireland. In the old days there were perhaps two or three Catholic magistrates out of a bench of 70. When he was Secretary for Ireland, he used his influence to secure the appointment of some 150 Catholic magistrates, and when Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster he appointed three working men. as 'justices of the Peace. Re condemned the system of plural voting, and said that, whether in or out of Parlia- ment, he would strive to abolish it. , The polling for the vacancy in the representation of Bridgeton Division of Glasgow, caused by the retirement of Mr. E. Russell (G.L.), opened on Tuesday morning, the candidates being Sir George Trevelyan (G.L.) and Mr. Evelyn Ashley (11. L. The result, which was expected to be declared by about 11 p.m., was awaited with consider- able interest, as both sides were putting forth their most strenuous efforts. The Cul-mist Liberals claimed that their canvass showed very promisingly for Mr. Ashley, while the Gladstonian Liberals expressed the utmost confidence in Sir George Trevelyan's return. There was much excitement locally, and plen- tiful signs of a contested election were seen. The weather being very fine, the poll was brisk during the first two hours. Both parties were well organised, and brought their men up rapidly, and the poll was expected to be the heaviest yet known. Vehicles of all kinds were brought into requisition, and the walls of the division were covered with electioneering placards, of which most were on behalf of Mr. Ashley. The Roman Catholic vote went solid for Sir George Trevelyan ; while the Orangemen to a man voted for Mr. Ash- ley. Since the register was made up there have been a great many removals, especially among the working- class oproters ; but the committees on both sides had traced most of them, and men were told off to bring them to the poll. Large numbers of operatives did not I, vote until between six and eight o'clock in the evening. As the day advanced the excitement increased. Very large crowds gathered around the polling stations, and the number of vehicles fetching and carrying elec- tors was great. Those employed on behalf of Sir George Trevelyan were chiefly spring carts, while Mr. Ashley's were waggonettes and carriages. At one polling sta- tion Sir George made a short speech, urging every elector to come to the poll and vote according to his' conscience tor the cause which would best prover the -c.ountry. Mr. Ashley-also delivered some encouraging words to his supporters at one polling sta- tion. A large number of workmen recorded their Votes during the dinner hour. The excitement attendant on the election was not confined to the Bridgeton Division alone, for in the Glasgow Royal Exchange and through- out the city every scrap of news about the polling was eagerly gathered. Business was practically suspended in the afternoon, and the streets near the polling stations were crowded with vehicles, as well as with men, women, and children. Two lurry loads of working , men were driven up amid loud cheers. The counting of the votes was conducted so expedi- tiously that the result was declared some time before the announcement was anticipated, and was received with immense enthusiasm. The figures were as follow:
TREVEI,YAI 4,654 ' ASFILEY

div.head: GENMI AL NEWS.
div.p: GENMI AL NEWS.

The ratification of the agreement for. the parcel post between England and France will be exchanges in a few days. The First Lord of the Treasury has intimated to Lord Claud Hamilton that the Government cannot hold out any hope that a day may he granted for a debate on the bounties question. The catch of herrings from Aberdeen to Lerwick up to Saturday for the present year amounts to 175,000 crane, as against 155,000 crans last year. The herring season is early this year, and is expected to go off quickly. The Shetland fishing is short. - - - -

_ A Florida farmer noticed two of his mulch cows fight- ing 'recently, and afterwards discovered that one had broken the other's neck, While their horns were so firmly interlocked as to require thuse of the dead cow to be sawn off before the livingone could be released.

At the coroners' inquests held in Yarmouth on the victims of the two boat accidents, the jury in both cases returned verdicts of accidental death, adding, however, in one case, that the disaster was due to the incompe- tence of the men in charge of the boat Dawn of Day. -----• ' - - -

News of the death of Major Hill, son of the late Captain Hill, of Knutsford, an old Waterloo veteran, which took place on Friday, at his residence. Middleton House, Knutsford, has been received in the district with profound regret. Major Hill was a magistrate for the county of Chester, and a Conservative in politics. Two young men were engaged in a prize fight at Glasgow Green on Saturday, when the police put in an appearance, and immediately the principals and their supporters made off. One of the pugilists, named Wm. Bell, aged 22, living in Nelson-street, Glasgow, in order ito escape the police, attempted to swim across the Clyde, but when within a few yards of the bank he sank and was drowned. His body was recovered an hour after- wards. . .

The terms of the draft charter for a new university, to be named the Albert University of London, and designed to include a district of fifteen miles' radius from Somer- set House, have been agreed upon and adopted by the Councils of University and King's Colleges, and will ac- cordingly be submitted to the Privy Council in a few days. The charter is in its essential features similar to that'of the Victoria University.

• JOSTLES GIFTS AND DEMONSTRATION.—There VMS A remarkable demonstration at Glossop on Saturday, wlieni the inhabitants made general holiday to celebrate recent munificent gifts to the town, which include a free library, • a hospital, and a park, the total value of the gifts' amounting to £50,000. The laving of the foundation stones of the proposed new buildings took place on Saturday in the presence of large gatherings, and a ban- quet, given by the Mayor, brought the proceedings of the day to a close. - -

THE- NORTHUMBERLAND MINFIRE AND THEIR REPRE- CHWATIVE.—The annual demonstration of the miners of Sorthumberland took place on Saturday at Myth Links, when the proceedings at times were very disor- derly owing to the ill-feeling engendered by the late strike, it being the opinion of some of the men that the officials of the association had not acted as they should have done. This feeling was particularly emphasised during the speech of the chairman. Mr. John Dixon, sPresident of the Northumberland Miners' Association, Who was subjected to a good deal of interruption.

HORRIBLE MURDER OE A Frail-WATCHER ITT POACRERS. —Archibald Reed, keeper for the local fishing associa- tion. was murdered at Tiverton, it is supposed, by poachers, early on Saturday. He left- home late on Friday, on information that four poachers were at work, and early on Saturday his body was found in the shal- low water of the river Exe. There were signs bf a Very severe struggle, and it was evident that he had first had his throat cut, and then been thrown into the river. The bottle industry is a very large one, the number produced per day in the respective countries being esti- mated as follows :—Great Britain and Ireland, 6,206 gross; Sweden, 960; Norway, 600; Denmark, 360; Ger- many and Belgium, 30,039; Austria, 7,000; France, 100; United States, 840; Canada, 120; Australia, 207; total, 46,432 gross. With 300 working days this gives no fewer than 15,929,600 gross per year. The Germans, by means of cheaper labour and more care in producing a sym- metrical bottle, absorb the great proportion of the trade at present. DESTIII7CTIVe FARM Fißlt.-13 IIoRSRS BURNED TO PRAM—About two am. On Monday, a fire broke out on the farm of West Mains or Huntly, came of Gowrie, Dundee, tenanted by Messrs. Henry Frain and Sons, and owing partly to an insufficient water supply the whole steading was consumed. By a great effort the cattle in the byres were rescued, but the fire had gained so strong a hold on the stables that 13 valuable horses were burned to death. A large quantity of grain and a new threshing mill were also destroyed. The damage, esti- matedi . at from £6,000 to £B,OOO, s covered by insurance. The cause of the fire is unknown.

CHILD Mt7HDEE AND CONCEALMENT AT CHEAbLE.: •—At the Chester Assizes on Saturday, before Justice Denman, Mary Ann Millington, 22, domestic servant, was indicted for the wilful mgrder of her child, five weeks old, at Cheadle, on the Sth inst. The prisoner lived Itt Stockport, and appeared to be fond of the child lit on the morning stated, when left alone, she drowned the little one in a tub, and afterwards concealed the body.. Medical evidence was called to show that at that time the prisoner was suffering from puerperal mania, and was at the time not responsible for her actions. The jury found the prisoner guilty of the act, hut also found that she was ingane at the time of its committal. She was ordered to he detained in custody until her Majesty's pleasure be known.

ANOTHER 'SWEETHEART MURDER AND SENTENCE OF , DRATH.—A youth named G. A. Early, only 18 years of age,' was sentenced to death at Winchester A ssizes, on Saturday, for the murder Of Isabella Rose Fleming, his sweetheart, at Southampton. /Co motive could be assigned for the crime, and the Judge, in reply to a suggestioa that the .1 shooting was accidental, said that defence had .never I been put forward. It was then said that the prisoner's .1 solicitor had advised him when before the magistrates to say nothing. The Judge said that if the solicitor H believed his client to be innocent, he had given him the I most pernicious advice that Was ever given in the world: The case was one which ought to he very closely inverg• tigated by the Horne Office, which might also profitably I occupy some portion of its time in considering whether or not the carrying of concealed weapons ought to be made an offence punishable with two years' hard labour.

THE QUEEN'S JUBILEE.—The Queen, acemnpanied by the Duke and Duchess of Connaught and Princesses Alice and Irene of 'Jesse, drove from, Osborne to West Cowes on Saturday. The occasion was Made A Jubilee Celebra- tion. The town was decorated, the school children were assembled, and a general holiday was observed. Fler • Majesty replied as follows to an address presented by the chairman of the Local Board :—" I thank you for your loyal and .dutiful address on the completion of the 50th year of my reign. It is a great satisfaction to me to find that my • people recognise and appreciate the many blessings which it has pleased God to bestow on this country since the beginning of My reign. My responaierl bilities• and anxieties have been -heavy and nutnerotia during this long period, and I feel deeply the continuous loyalty of my faithful subjects which leads thetn to asso- ciate their present prosperity with myself amithe fulfil-, !tient of the duties of my sovereignty." TERRIBLE RAILWAY ACC Wl*: T TN -A USTR ALIA. The Queen's Jubilee Day in Australia NV11.9 marked by a most terrible railway disaster, in ornich five persons were killed outright and many injured. Particulars of the catastrophe have just been received by the Australian mail. From these it appears that the Queen's Jubilee was held at Sydney on the 21st June, and on that day an excursion took place to the tlavrkesbury river. A train left Sydney in the inorning vrith about4loo extursionists. On arriving at a very steep hill the engine was unable to pull the entire train, and it had ti go Up in two seetions. These were made up again when the top of the incline was reached. The decline on the opposite side was.very steep and continuous. The engine could not Control the carriages, which forced it along at a terrible: rate. It was said that the train at this moment attained,X speed of 70 miles an hour, and the passeugers became greatly alarmed at the fearful pace. The engine dtiver did all he could to apply the brakes, as did also the guard, but they had no power. The train was quicklyapproachitiv a great danger, viz.. Peats ferry, where the river is situated. The pointsman here, st sing the train coming at the terrific rate, turned it on to a siding where there were some carpenters' trucks on the lino. This .saved the train dashing into another one waiting at the station; but. as it was, the two first carriages were tele- scoped. The shrieks and screams of the excursionists were appalling. Three were killed in the carriages. The engine rolled over the embankment into the thud, bury- ing the poor engine-driver. Another man on the engine was also killed. A great number of the people were in- jured, and it was marvellous that there were but five ' deaths

A BOLTON DIVORCE CASE.—The netion of Shollcross v :3hellcross and Cross, which was undefended, came before Sir Jas. flannen, the president of the court, on Saturday. The petitioner, who is a chemist's assistant at Bolton, prayed for a divorce on account of his wife's adultery with a person named William Cross, of Bolton. From the opening statement of Mr. 11. M. Middieton, it appeared that the parties were married at the Registrar's office, in Bolton, last year, and that ,they after- wards cohabited at Nelson-street, Bolton, and Liverpool. For a time the petitioner and his wife lived happiiy together, but when she formed an attachment with the co-respondent, Cross, there were quarrels. The respondent confessed to her husband that she had seen intimate with Cross, the co-respondent, at an hotel in Manchester, and the petitioner, without delay, instituted these proceedings. The petitioner was examined in support of the case. Be said his wife confessed the adultery with Cross, and she added that she liked Cross better than she liked him. On the Bth of January last the corespondent and a man drove up in a; cab to witness's home in Latimer-street. The man came to the door, and said to witness, within the hearing. of CTOSS, 4We don't want you, but we want your wife." (Laughter.) On the 19th of March last witness and his wife were at her mother's house together, and Cross came in, and asked Mrs. Shellcross if witness was her husband, and she replied, "Yes."—Thomas Wood, a retired ser- geant of police, said he had served the citation on both parties.—The President said the evidence Was sufficient to justify the Court in granting a dee,ree nisi, which he now pronounced, with coats.

WRECK AND Loss ov EIGHT LIVES.—A telegram from Stanley, vid Monte Video, reports that the British ship Star of Scotia, from San,Francisco for Queenstown, is totally wrecked on Bull Point. The first officer and seven of the crew *ere drowned.

Daowtaxa FATALITY.—At flude,an Monday, Mr. James Palmer, of Saltash, corn dealer, also a local preacher of the Baptist Connexion, while bathing with two friends was drowned. His body was recovered seine hours after- wards. The deceased leaves a wife and fatnitk.

At the conference of the Association for the Reform of the Law of Nations a resolution was adopted to the effect that all eiVilised nations should enter into mutual en- gagements to submit to arbitration all questions arising Out of the interpretation of existing treaties and conven- tions.

Lord Delanaere died at Vale Royal, Northwich, Cheshire, on Monday, in his 76th year, The deceased, who leaves a widow and a sennnd daughter, sat as the Conservative member forDenbiglishire and Montgomery kora 1840 to 1847. He vra3 lion. colonel of the Cheshire ..Regiment, 3rd battalion, and was twice married. ' An application was made to Mr. Justice Chitty for an • interim injunction to restrain the proprietors of the American Exhibition from craatirig a nuisance by noise and smell by Buffalo Bill's Wild West. Affidavits from several of the neighbours, who declared that they had not suffered any annoyance or inconvenience, were pro- duced for the defence, and the further hearing was adjourned. , ;A FACTORY STRUCK lIY LIGHTNINO.—A thunderstorm passed over the neig,hbourhood 'of Rochdale on Sunday afternoon, and the electric fluid from one terrific explo- sion struck th.t chimney of Clegg Hall cotton mill, knocking off eight yards of the top and setting fire to me cotton cotton in the building in four different parts. A 'number of workpeople were soon at the scene and ex-- tinguished the flames before much damage was done. w • Tun NEW RAILWAY BRIDGE ACROSS THE DRE.—lifr. Gladstone will place the first cylinder in position for the new railway bridge across the 'DPP, near Connah's Quag..+4ll on the 16th inst. This bridge will be constructed ky Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire Railway Corn-' pany, and will give the whale of the coal fields and mineral districts of North Wales, capable of producing four million tons per annum, direct. access with the Mar- . sey and the manufacturing districts of the north of Eng. ;land, by means of the lines of the Midland. Great North- ern, and Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire com- panies, composing the Cheshire Lines Committee, by which the new extension will be worked.

SERIOUS RATLVY Accinenr : 30 NiI:MED.—A Colli.• sion occurred on Monday evening on the North-Eastern 'Railway at Forth Banks, close to the Tnfirmary at New- , castle. A train of empty North British carriage,s was being brought into the Central Station to take out an T excursion train and collided with a workman's train from the West. There were between 20 and 30 persons - injured. One man had both his legs broken, and another ri had one leg broken, whilst a third received a severe cut in the head, and several were badly shaken. A number • of the injured were removed to the Infirmary on 'r stretchers, and others with m nor injuries walked to the 7 institution and had their wounds dressed. The affair caused a slight panic among the passengers standing on the platforms at the Central Station. Mr. Godfrey Smith, passenger superintendent, and Mr. Reid, station- master, were in the station at the time of the occurrence. They were quickly on the scene, and gave directions for the removal of the injured, and took the necessary measures for the resumption of traffic so that the line I, was soon cleared. _,l CIIFSIII RE LINES EXTENSION RAILWAY.—The report.' of the directors of the Southport and Cheshire .1 Lines Extension Railway for the half-year ending ' • 30th June, just issued, slates that the gross receipts amounted to £6,933 ss. 9d., as cmnpared with £5,996 ' • 12s. for the corresponding period of last year, showing an increase of £936 13s. 9d. The directors regretted' that the company had been put to the expense of a Par- ' liarnentary opposition to a bill introduced by the Liver- pool, Southport, and Preston Junction Company in the present session; in the result the interests of the Exten- sion Company were sustained. The efforts of the directors to close the capital account RS early as possible were being continued. Of the 2,500 shares surrendered by the contractor, 300 had been disposed of in settlement of claims against the company,

On Surldty, a shocking case of wife murder oecurred at Bollibn, where a man named Thomas Matthews, about employed as a bricklayer, and residing at Farnworth, kicked his wife Ellen, aged about 29, to death in Back Irving-street. It appears that Mat theWs is a militiaman, and had been 'to Bury for training for the last week or two. He returned on Saturday. but instead of going home to Earhworth, he proceeded to Brownlowfold, Bolton where he spent some time and money drinking. On Saturday his wife, hearing of his return, went to 'Bolton and saw him. He then gave her 14s. She had with her her two children, a girl of four and a baby in arms. • She stayed all night at the house of a Mrs. Murray in Irving-street. On Sunday afternoon, whilst Matthews was sitting in a house in the same street, with a. man named Crook, Mrs. Matthews went to him, and there was an altercation about the 14s. She said she would have more money or brain him with.a stone. Matthews refused to give her more, and she then left, but soon returned with her little girl, saying—" This is a bricklayer's daughter." This a ppears to have exasperated Matthews, who attacked his wife by kicking her on the head, killing her instantly. Matthews immediately went away. The police gave chase to Matthews. and arrested him in the Roman Catholic chapel yard. Both the man and woman had been drinking heavily during the day. When apprehended Matthews told the policeman as be was proceeding to the police office that he did not know that he had killed his wife, and when he went away he lay down in a field, end a man Cattle and told him that his wife was dead. He then went to the priest, intending afterwards to give himself up:

GLAGGow having done nobly, Liberal Eng- land expects that every Liberal ekector in the Northwich Division of Cheshire will do nis duty. The issue is fortunately as simple in the county as it waG in the city Division; it is the question of the government of Ire- ' I land. Mr. J. T. BRUNNER, as the Liberal candidate, believes in Conciliation; Lord HENRY GROSVENOR, as a Liberal Unionist, 'stands for Coercion. In the Address which .he has this week issued, his :lordship says he will "uphold the authority of the Executive," and "insist on that regard for the obser- vance of the law which is the surest guaran- tee of prosperity under the democratic institu- tions which we possess." In other words a, Coercion Bill having become the law of the land, Lord HENRY pledges hiniself to sup- port a policy of coercion. It is nothing, it seems, to him, that the eighty-six Coercion Acts that have previously been passed have proved anything but "guarantees of pros- perity,'' but have, on the contrary, deeply impoverished and shamefully degraded Ire- land. He is an inexperienced young man, and will doubtless have to stumble many times before he gets his feet on the right path; but that is no ieason why those should follow him who have learned to walk aright. He pledges himself to uphold the Unionist Government of which Lord SALIS !BURY is the head; and be ought to be re- minded, when he commits himself so readily to Coercion, that the Piumtt MINIS- TER himself said, when questioned as to his wisdom in allowing the Crimes Act to lapse, that that Act—a Coercion Act—would create ten times as much evil as it would repress. Does Lord HENRY GRoSVENOR be- lieve this ? and, if so, how can he expect the eltotors of Cheshire to return him to Parlia- ment? Ireland has suffered terribly in the past through the miserable wrong doing cl lords Led lordlings ; and Englishmen are , now, it is to be hoped, too wise to send young aristocrats to Parliament to increase the evil. They prefer rather to put their conscience in the keeping of such men as Mr. BRUNNER, who preach and practice peace on earth and 'goodwill to men. Mr. BRUNNER has clear views, and has run a straight course on the Irish question. Referring in his present Address to the statement he made when he was elected as the first Parliamentary repre- sentative of the Northwich Division, he says: —" At that time I had openly declared to you my opinion that Ireland ought to have full power to deal with all affairs purely Irish, but that I would be no party to any enact- ment which would make the two millions of Irish people living in Great Britain foreigners amongst us.' " He redeemed his pleige in this matter by voting in favour of Mr. GLAD- STONE'S Home Rule scheme—holding with its author that in thus voting he was not com- mitting himself to more than the principle of the bill. It ought to be a satisfaction to the Liberal. Unionists of the Division to know that Mr. BRUNNER is opposed to the exclu• sion of the Irish members from Westminster, and that he will not be a party to supporting any scheme for buying out the Irish land- lords which involves risk to the British taxpayer. Indeed, the Liberal Unionists are so well met by the Liberal candidate and by Mr. GLADSTONE, as the leader of the Liberal party, that we are puzzled to know what reason they can give for hesitating to i vote for the candidate selected by the Liberal ' party. Mr. BRUNNER mikes a stiong point of the fact that the Tories and their allies at the last election promised "to govern Ireland by the same laws as Great Britain " ; and , this pledge having been " shamelessly 'broken, he asks the electors to punish this breach of faith by returning him at the head of the poll. We have little doubt that a satis- factory response will, on Saturday next, be made to this appeal. There is every pros- pect that the Liberal candidate will be triumphant; but we would urge the Liberals of the Division to work with such ardour and enthusiasm as will ensure Mr. BRUNNER the Iround thousand of a majority by which he was first returned to Parliament.

IT is satisfactory to see that, in the inter- vals of party strife, attention is being directed to the higher education of the people of this country so as to put them on a level with their Continental competitors. Mr. SMITH an- nounced in the House of Commons, on Mon- day, that the Technical Education Bill was one of the few measures which the Govern- ment hoped to be able to place upon the sta- tute book during the present session. It is a moot question with many people whether the pace is not getting too quick in the matter of education ; but the answer is that we must either keep up with our neighbours or be left behind. It is certainly unwise to put chil. dren when at school through a "forcing" process ; and parents who find that the health of their little ones is suffering through over pressure are in duty bou-id to see to it that some of the pressure is taken off. Thanks to our compulsory system of elementary edu-1 cation, we are now managing exceedingly ' well in the early stages. It is in the outfit for the advanced stage that our deficiency is apparent. It is not at all an uncommon thing for a German, or a Frenchman, to be employed by English merchants as foreign correspondent, and this, not because the merchant has a preference for a foreigner— rather the reverse—but because there are so few Englishmen, in the walks of commerce, who understand any language but their own. It is lamentable that this is so ; but it is for- tunately a defect which can be remedied, for there is no inaptitude on the part of Englishmen to acquire foreign languages. I What is wanted is a course of training in this direction as part of the ordinary equipment for commercial life. A suggestion has been made that there should be Colleges of Com- merce which should make provision for the study of modern languages; and the idea is a good one, for it ma.7-,T be said to cover an important branch of Technical leducation. In this connection, Mr. LINCOLN CHANDLER has written a letter to the "London Iron Trade Exchange" and, from the copy which we give of it in another column, it will be seen he refers to what Mr. THOMAS MORRIS has done in Warrington in order to encourage the study of the German language. All honour to Mr. MORRIS ' for the help he has given, but we hold that it ought not to be left to the private efforts of individuals to fit our young men •for the great industrial struggle which is obviously before us. The State and the Municipality should be lending what aid they can—and lending it systemati- cally and thoroughly. To this end Free Libraries should be free in lac: as well as in

name. illut perhaps we are over-stepping the line when we say "Libraries," for we be- lieve Warrington is the only town in the Kingdom which, after levying a penny in the pound ,on-the ratepayers for the maintenance of a " Free !Library," has the audacity to break the law by imposing a subscription, in addition, !before a ratepayer can take a book home to read. Mr. MORRIS recently offered, on certain conditions, to provide £5OO as a means of helping the Library Com- mittee out of the rut into which they have floundered; bat, as they have refused the off?r, it is now withdrawn so far as Mr. MORRIS is concerned. The Library Corn niittee will shortly be called upon to put their, own shoulders to the wheel, or, if they will not do that, they will be asked to step aside, and make way for ,others who are more able or more willing than they to do the work that requires to be done. If Parliament is willing, as it seems to be, to open the door to tech- nical education, the least that can be done in a town like Warrington, where there is a well stocked library, is to give students ordinary help by letting them read the books by "their own firesides. A barrier in the shape of a subscription is illegal, and because it is illegal it is tyrannical, and because it is tyrannical it should be resisted and broken down.

div.p: "TOUCH AND GO."

Wellington was spoken of by Byron as the Prince of Cut-throats; but to-day the litle might be more aptly applied to the Crown Prince of Germany, considering the w,y in which his throat is being dealt with by eminent surgeons.

"The Liberal Ifnionist," which has hitherto been published weekly, will for the future be published monthly. This is pro- gress as it is understood amongst the Liberal Unionists. After a while we may look to its being issued quarterly, and then—not at all.

Sir John Lubbock deserves to be had in crateful remembrance as the author of the Bank Holiday Act. Monday last was a glorious day, and made a million people happy. When Sir John passes off the scene, he ough t to be enshrined in tip; calendar as St. Lub- bock. He deserves canonisation as well as some of the saints.

The death of Mr. Robert Verdin, while casting a deep gloom over Northwich, has served to show how the good qualities of a good man endear him to his neighbours. The poet Shirley was right when he said : Only the actions of the just Smell sweet and blossom in the dust.

The projected duel between General Bou- langer and M. Ferry has ended in a ridicu- lous collapse. The seconds could not agree as to the conditions of he fight, and so there has to be no fight at all. This is better than pu..ting a bullet in a body; but it would be better still if the Fiend) could bring them- selves to laugh duelling out of existence, as has been done in this country.

The " Times" thinks the Scotch electors have given Sir George Trevelyan a large majority because "the policy of Ministers has not yet been carried into effect in a thorough-going way." This means that the Coercion Act has to be put in force by sup- pressing the National League. The "Times" asks the Government, as things are going hard with them, to seek salvation by corn- mitting suicide.

Four lads, who had been bathing in New- ton Lake, were summoned for" maliciously trespassing." It was contended that the trespass was not malicinus, and that custom sanctioned bathing in the lake. The magis- trates dismissed the cases. "as there seemed to be some doubt :" but intimated that boys had no right to go where they did. This would appear to be equivalent to a verdict of "Not guilty this time, but you will be guilty if you do it again."

Same of the members of the St. Helens Town Council think it unwise to give de- tails in their sanitary reports as to the con- dition of Sankey Brook. Perhaps so, for as gaol•birds are told—" What you now say will be taken down in evidence against you." The really wise thing to do would be to set about the task of purifying the brook. It is a vile uncovered sewer—an abomination to the nose and eve of man and beast. Those who have to cross it may say as Coleridge said of the river at Cologne : I counted two-and-seventy stenches, All well defined and different stinks !

How absurd of the Tories of the Northwich Division to make a fuss because Mr. Brunner wrote a private letter or two respecting the election before the interment of the late mem- ber. Did the Tories do nothing prior to the fcmeral, or was it by a piece of magic that within a couple of hours of the interment, they had Lord Henry Grosvenor in attendance to deliver a speech as their candidate?

Mr. J H. Cooke acted the part of the can. did friend in telling the Tories and their allies that "they must remember that they had a great many fortuitous circumstances in their favour at the tut elce ion wi.iich might probably not be exercised at the prwn t one." Just so; and how frank he is in teCOV- nising the alliance of the Tories and Dissen- tient Liberals as a fortuitous circumstance." But that alliance is breaking down the Dis- sentients are dissenting. They do not like tar of the Tory orush, and they are begin- ning to wash themselves clean.

" I shall be entirely at your service to pro- mote and further the salt trade." This is how Lord Henry Grosvenor tries to snare the little birds of Northwich. He is a juven- ile angler, and fresh from home. When he has been round and about a little more, he will find that story about catching birds by putting salt on their tails is a story.

Lord Henry Grosvenor says it is cant and humbug to talk of coercion; for, be adds, if you give a man nasty medicine in order to effect a recovery, it does not follow that you coerce him. Quite true, my lord, but what should we say if a doctor forced the same nasty medicine down a patient's throat 86 times, in spite of his protests. and notwith• standing the fact that every dose made him worse? Should we not say that he was a fool or a quack ? Or would it be better to say it was all cant and humbug "to expect a cure? Eh, my lord ?

Samuel Stanley, whose case'was first called on, hoped that the mag- istrates would be as lenient as they possibly could; he did not believe in vaccintitinn. 'ELECTION OF ASSISTANT OVERSEER AT PENKETH. —Yesterday afternoon the election df an assistant overseer to fill the vacancy caused by the death of the late Mr. T. Garnett took place at Penketh. The two candidates for the office were Mr. T. H. Wilson and Mr. B. Hobson. The poll was opened at four o'clock and closed at eight, the ,polling place being the Conservative Club. Mr. Jonas Forster, the senior overseer, was the presiding officer, and the poll clerk was Mr. S. Sutton. Shortly after the close of the poll the presiding officer announced to the people, who had gethered in considerable num- ber at the outside of the club, that the result of the poll was as follows :—Mr. Wilson, 151 votes ; Mr. Hobson, 69. Mr. Wilson was, therefore, declared to have been elected. The event caused a good deal of excitement in the village, though the contest was carried on in the most amicable manner.
