div.head: OUR LONDON LErfER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LErfER.
LONDON. THIJRBDAX.

The result of the Glasgow election is a further proof of the steady advance of the growing power of Liberalism throughout the country. Its signifi- cance is so marked and unmistakeable that; to do the Conservative press justice, they, with very few exceptions, more or less ungraciously admit it. Sir George Trevelyan was not an ordinary candidate. He was in himself a prominent example of the decay of the revolt which a year ago weakened the hands of Mr. Gladstone, and delayed the inevitable rendering of justice to Ireland. He had been a Dis- sentient. He had seen the error of his ways, frankly acknowledged it, and now came before a large and representative constituency to ask them what they thought of the question. The answer has been given by returning him with a majority exceeding anything polled in the division since it was created. This election has recalled the old gossip about the imminence (If a General Election. Some authorities go so far as e 0 declare that it is really settled upon, and will take place this, autumn. I do not think there is the slightest foundation for the apprehen- sion. There are two influential parties able to ad- vance weighty reasons against such a course. One is headed by Lord Hartington and Mr. Chainberlain, who say they will do all in their power to avert a General Election in accordance with their pledge to stand by the Government. who would certainly be turned out if the election•took place. The Govern-, meat, on the other hand, shake their head and. , gravely say it would be a breach of faith on their part to hasten a General Election which would in- evitably result in the Dissentient Liberals being decimated. Between these two points of view we get an accurate outlook on the situation. The recent elections prove that the brief day of the Dissentient Liberals is over, and if they were rejected by the constituencies where they hold perilous seats the Government, even if their supporters were returned , in undiminished force, would be in a decided minority, and must needs resign office. Mr. Chamberlain, it is well known, had another plan in hand which made him momentarily indif- ferent to the fate of the Government or the fortunes of Mr. Gladstone. In his mind's eye he saw "A National Party," of which he was to be dictator, with some semblance of power conceded to Lord Randolph Churchill.. But this castle in the air has come down with a run, and nothing has. been heard of the national party for f ally a week. In- deed, there have been signs of dissension between the two eminent men of whom, with perhaps Mr. Jesse Collings, the "party" consisted. On Monday night the House of Commons was delighted to find Mr. Chamberlain attacking Lord Randolph Church- ill with the certain result of Lord Randolph turning fiercely upon his whilom associate. Scarcely. less significant was Lord Hartington's action in refusing to desert the Government upon the issue raised. Whether this estrangement is only temporary re- mains to be, seen. There is no doubt that a few weeks ago Mr. Chamberlain and Lord Randolph Churchill were con-piring to create a "party" which they should lead, and were willing to sacri- fice the present Government or anything else to effect their purpose. Recruits coming in very slowly, the two inventors of the "party" have taken to falling out with each other. Mr. Smith, asked the other night, could not sayl when the session would be over. One thing grows increasingly certain, and that is that the session will see us into September. But though the House sits with regularity, and even manages upon occa- sion to present a crowded appearance, the Whips could tell a depressing story of the increasing num- ber who are taking French leave. The demand for pairs is pressing and prevailing. , If the market were the Stock Exchange, and transactions were reported, the value of a pair whuld be found to have gone far above par. At the outset the Conservative Whips set their faces sternly against assisting in the transaction of forming pairs. But members, deprived of this agency, undertook the business themselves, and are carrying it through with great success. Now that the Land Bill is practically through, ministerialists who have borne the hest and burden of the day think they have earned the privilege of a heliday, and, in any case, are taking it. 'Next week Mr. Gladstone retires from the field, not because he is either wounded or fatigued, for he looks a great deal better at the end of the session than lie did at its commencement, but because he thinks it a grave duty to preserve his health and strength for the opportunity of completing his great work, which no seems within measurable distance. The chief impression created in the public mind by the announcement of the death of Henry May- hew was one of surprise that he should be still alive. Born eighty-five years ago, he was in his prime between 1840 and 1850. Since then, a new generation has taken possession of the world, and Henry Mayhew's name is only dimly recalled as a worker in that field which Walter Besant has more recently cultivated. What promises to be an un- fortunate controversy has arisen on the question 1 whether Mayhew ever was an editor of "Punch." The statement has been put forward by his son and is gently contradicte 1 in the current number of "Punch," which has led to a more detailed account being supplied by the son as to his father's connec- tion with the famous periodical. The fact of the matter is there is no one living who can speak with personal authority on the subject. On the present staff of "Punch' there is only one whose connec- tion with the paper runs forty years, and the paper was already two years old when he joined it. At that time Mark Lemon was editor. But the state- ment made on behalf of Henry Mayhew refers to the first year of the paper's existence. On this point it is interesang to refer to Mayhew's personal authority, which may be presumed to have supplied the material for the notice of him in "Men of the Time." It is there written that in 1841 he was "one of the promoters of 'Punch,' from which he afterwards withdrew." There is no mention here of his having been editor. When I was down at Portmouth for the Naval Review, I had communicated to me under pledges of secresy strictly kept, the story of the narrow escape from a watery grave of a distinguished com- pany of literary Men and artists, the latter includ- ing one of the most popular of workers in black and white. But as the story is now running through the clubs, with fanciful additions, there can be no harm in giving the simple version of the facts. The party had engaged a steam launch with intent to cruise about. They carried out this intention with characteristic liberality, crossing the line at all pro- hibited points, and drawing down upon them a chorus of ohjurgations from irate authorities on the ironclads. At last things began to grow so hot that the captain lost his head, and in attempting to weather the bow of an ironclad ran right into her The ironclad did not seem at all affected by the circumstance, but the steam launch shipped a good deal of water which to the fevered imagina- ,tion gave rise to the cry that she was sinking. A rope was thrown over from the iron- clad, towering like the dome of St. Paurs Cathe- dral over the launch. "I'll show you the way out," said an eminent novelist, and was as good as his word, swarming up the rope till he was landed on the ironclad, from the deck of which he surveyed the scene below. Another tried the rope, but had not swarmed up many feet when his power of pro- pulsion gave out, and after some' momenta of an- guished suspense he came flop, back again into the launch. Another, also a novelist, tried with even leas success, for in descending he dropped into the sea, whence he was rescued amid a scene of great excitement. By this time someone had discovered that the launch was not leaking, and that the water plenteously shipped at the time of the collision had come over the gunwale. Confidence was quickly restored, and what threatened to end in a tragedy came to be regarded as an excellent joke, highly
conducive to the day's enjoyment. The comrad on the ironclad was let down again by the rope and the launch steamed off, the half-drowned nove7 I list getting his clothes dried by degrees.

NORTilVirieff DIVISION ELECTIONe MR. BRUNNER'S CANDIDATURE. In the Bethesda Schoolroom, Runcorn, on Satur- day. the members of the Council of the Division Liberal Association met for the purpose of deciding what course should be adopted with reference to the representation of the division. Mr. J. R. Frith was voted to the chair. There was a capital atten- dance of delegates. The Chairman said it was with feelings of great regret that he was called upon to attend a meeting of Liberals at the present time owing to the sad death of our late member Mr. Verdin. (Hear, hear.) Whilst disagreeing with Mr. Verdin in politics, he always looked upon him as a straightforward, hon- ourable man, and a man who deserved the confidence of everyone. Mr. A. E. Fletcher ,•ead a number of letters he had received. Their esteemed president, Mr. E. H. Moss, of Middlewich, -was as cordial with them as ever, and expressed his deep regret that he could not be present that night. He assured them that he would give the party his hearty support in the contest in which they were about to engage. (Applause.)— The_ Rev. G. A. Walker, of Middlewich, wrote that if the Council selected Mr. Brunner as the candidate that would meet the wishes of the electors of Middlewich, and he should be glad, personally, to do all he could in his small sphere to secure his return to Parliament at the proper time. (Applause.) Mr. Sproston asked Mr. Flet- cher to assure the Council of the continuance of loyalty of the South-eastern portion of the Division to the Association and to Mr. Brunner. (Applause.) He hoped they would invite Mr. Brunner to be the candidate and nothing would stop them from re- turning him as their member. (Applause.) Mr. Pickering (Winsford), wrote that providence hav- ing removed our late friend, their duty was to find a better man to succeed him. Such a gentleman they had ready to h.ind and he did not for a second suppose that the Council would read the alphabet further than the second letter. In the hearts of thousands of people in the division "B" stood for Brunner. (Applause.) Mr. Slater of Woodford Hall also wrote apologising for non-attendance, and said there wou'd be no diihculty in finding a candidate to suit the Liberals of this district. Mr. Brunner then came forward, and received a most enthusiastic welcome. Addressing- those Pre- sent as "My old friends" he moved the following resolution, "That the Council of Northwich Liberal Association hereby expresses their sincere regret at the death of Robert Verdin, Esq., member for the Division and respectfully tender their great sym- pathy to his sorrowing relatives in their sad be- reavement. (Hear, hear.) He said he belieVed that there was no man in that division outside the circle of his immediate relatives who had felt with a keener and a deeper sorrow the death of Mr. Robert Verdin than he had. (Hear, hear.) He had gone through perhaps the greatest sorrow that could fall upon a man and he could feel for the brothers and for the sister. What a loss it Wee to pert from one who bad been dear to them ever since they had drawn breath. (Hear, hear.) He had looked forward to meeting Mr. Vordin in perfect health and to shaking hands with him in a friendly way,both before and after an honest political tight. (Hear, hear.) It had not to be, God in his providence had removed from amongst them a man who Was a good host, a good neighbour, a good master, and a rood brother a large minded and a great man. He moved thia resolution with a sad pleasure, that they tendered their respectful sympathy to his sorrowing relatives. Mr. S. C. Beckett seconded the motion. He might say in truth that when the news of Mr. Verdin's death arrived at Runcorn the entire population was shocked. Such a calamity wits never expected, and he thought it was right that the Council should express sympathy with the family. There was no doubt that Mr. Verdin was a man highly re- garded and respected in this division, otherwise he would not have won a victory on the last occasion. (Hear, hear.) He was elected purely because he was regarded so very highly by the whole division, and they all regretted his un- timely death. The resolution was unantmously carried in silence; and Mr. Brunner then retired from the room. Mr. H. Bratt (Northwich) moved with great pleasure, "That the Council of the Northerich Division Liberal As- sociation hereby affirm their confidence ir their late repre- sentative. J. T. Brunner, Ees—(cheers),—and respectfully I requests him to again contest the division as the candidate' of the Association at the ensuing elem ion. (Cheers ) They had, be said, known Mr. Brunner for a long time, and the best of it was they knew his principles. (Hear, hear.) It was not a matter of the man but the principles of the man that recommended Mr. Brunner to them. (Cheers.) Mr. Brunner was the right man, and especially must they con- sider him so when they remenshered that he was a firm sup- porter of the man who for fully half a century had done more for the people of this country than any other man living. (Cheers.) Be could tell them what they intended to do in Northwich, and he was sorry to say that they rather neglected it at the last election—they intended to work. (Hear, hear.) They intended to work and carry Mr. Brunner, for the reason that this election was of the greatest importance to Mr Gladstine. (Hear, hear.) The eyes of England, Scotland, Ireland. and Wales were upen this con- test, and they must Win. (Cheers.) Mr Hulme (Middlewich) seconded the motion. Be knew of no man that had won his way, or was more likely to win his way into their hearts, as the one whose name had I been proposed for adoption. (Hear, hear.) At the last elec- lion mistakes were made; there was coldness and Apathy where there should have been warmth and energy, and the lesson they had to learn from par experience was not to be over confident. (Hear, hear ) There was nothing more uncertain in life than a petit cal c ntest, unless it were a horse race. (Laughter.) Let them work hard to return Mr Brunner by a majority of 1,600, and then they could shake bands with him and wish him prosperity, which, he hoped, lay before him as a supporter of the Grand Old Man. (Cheers ) The Chairman said that at the present time they wanted a man who had no uncertain sound about him—(cheere)— and he thought that the men of Northwich and Runcern would put their shoulders to the wheel and try to send a man who would stand by Mr Gladstone, and see right and justice done. (Cheers ) By a mere accident, he (the chair- man) had the pleasure of proposing Mr Brunner's candide- tore on the first occasion, and that led to victory. He WAS glad to he able to lend his voice on the present occasion for sendine him a rcond time. (Cheers) From what he could gather there was no lukewartnness amongst the Liberals of the division; they wore heart and soul in the cause; and he WAS sure that if they were victory would be theirs. (Cheers.) Were they all determined to use their individual eff mts in the right way to secure Mr Brunner's return. (Loud cries of "Yes.") The resolution was carried by loud acclamatione,and upon Mr. Brunner re-entering the room the audience roes to their feet and'cheered him most heartily. The Chairman haying informed him of the decision of the meeting, Mr. Brunner said he had been reading the newspapers lately, and he gathered from those that he saw that it ap- peared to be the unanimous opinion of all political parties that they would adopt him that day—(laughter)—and, therefore, he summoned up courage to come by train, leav- ing Hartford that afternoon. (Cheers.) Would they allow him, before he said another word, to ask his friend Mr. Fletcher to read the address he (Mr. Brunner) propesed to issue to the electors. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Fletcher then read the address, and be was frequently interrupted by cheers. Mr. Brunner, resuming, said it was not a usual thing far a preacher to get somebody to read his text for him, but he trusted they would believe that it was a good text. (Hear, hear.) In fact there was many a text, and he had no doubt that if, by his speeches, he stuck to his text he should be able to convert a minority into a majority. (Che-rs.) He was there that day in the first place most thankfully to ac- cept their offer. (Cheers.) Many of those present knew that after the election 12 months ago, he was repeatedly I asked to turn back upon them and go to a place where the flatterers said he had a better chance. (Laughter.) He re- fused those effete for the reason that he fele it to be his clearest and moet iniperative duty not to refuse to stand by the men who would stand by him. (Cheers.) However, shortly after that election, after exceedingly bard work, he went away for a most enjoyable holiday, It was about three weeks since he came home an the first thing he heard was the news of the Spalding election. He heare other good news since that day, and he wanted them to add another to those victories-(cbeers)-to cheer Mr. Gladstone's heart. (Re- newed cheers.) He accepted their offer, and he undertook before them that day not to spare himself one matnent until victory be won. (Cheers.) He did not know whether they were aware of it, but it WM a fact that he had never asked a workman in Cheshire for his Tote. He had ben too proud ever to make it a personal matter between the voter and himself that he should vote for him. He had always en- deavoured to lav before the electors the highest possible motives that occurred to him to induce them to give their votes in his favour. Now he was going to ask in addition, "If you love me, vote for me. (Cries of "We will.") They had a very serious task before them, and he did not want them to disguise the fact from themselves. They were a party in a minority.. Runcorn people voted fairly Liberal, at any fate the men who did vote, but there was a very large abstention in Runcorn, and he had to ask the men who were to work in Runcorn to bring those who ab- stained to their side, not only with their sympathy, but with their work and h.arty support and with their X at the end of the election. MANCHESTER SHIP, CANAL.

On Thursday,- the- Manchester Ship Canal Com- pany raid to the Bank of England, by arrangement with the Bridgewater Navigation Company, Limi- ted, the sum of £1,710,000, being the amount of the purchase money of the Bridgewater Canal and Mer- sey and Irwell Navigation. These undertakings are, therefore, the property of the Manchester Ship Canal Company, whose Directors intend to carry them on as hitherto, and the continuity of the business of general carriers will be maintained. At a special meeting of the shareholders of the Bridgewater Navigation Company, held, yesterday week, the Chairman (Mr.Janies Cropper) announced that on Thursday, according to notice which the directors had received, the purchase of the concern by the Manchester Ship Canal Company would be completed and the money paid. The announcement was received _wi,th cheers. The Bridgewater Navi- gation Compafty, Mr. Cropper addedr had now sim- ply to repay to theshareholders the caßital they had invested. The total amount 'of 'capital .upon . paid-up ordinary shares, £lO preference shares, and bonds owing by the company was £887,578; and they were to receive from the Ship Canal Company £1,710,000. This left a sum of £822,322 to be divi- ded amongst the different classes of shareholders in such manner as might be directed by the court. He inbred a resolution tothe effect that, having heard the statement as to the-expected purchase, the di- rectors be empowered to take steps as soon as prac- ticable for winding up the company, and to call a'special meeting for that purpose. The resolution was carried unanimously. The &motors were authbrised to apply any, sum not exceeding £lB,OOO out of the funds of the company in making com- pensation to the officers and servants of the company in consequence of their loss of employ- ment by the sale of the concern to the Ship Canal Company. At a meeting of the Salford Town Council, held on Wednesday, Mr. Foden moved the falowing re- solution :—" That this Council heartily congratu- lates the directors of the Ship Canal Company on the suecess which has attended their efforts in over- coming the difficulties in connection, with the financial arrangements to raise the capital for carry- ing out their great enterprise, which has the pro- mise of such vast and important benefits to the commercial and manufacturing interests of the inhabitants of Manchester and Salford, and the immense population of" the surrounding districts." Mr. Foden sketched the history of the endeavours to establish water communication between Manchester and Liveryool. Ile said that the Corporation of Sal- ford had always been honourably connected with the efforts to push the scheme forward, and it was right that they should adopt such a resolution as. he proposed. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. Alderman Walmsley seconded the resolution, and remarked that they could claim for themselves that they, had 'nursed this great scheme in its infancy.—Mr. Alderman Dickins asked whether the £5,000 which the Conn- ell gave in support of the scheme would now be repaid in money, or whether the Council would be- come a shareholder to the extent of the money it had paid.—Mr. Alderman Husband replied that Air. Alderman Dickins and all the Council knew that in the event of the scheme 'being successfully floated it was in the option of the Council ts decide , whether their money should be paid back or whether they should accept the alternative of taking shares in the scheme to the amount of the SUM advanced. These conditions remained unaltered at the present moment. Before the Council coulddo, anything it would be necessary that ,the subject should be brought up and discussed.—The resolution was unanimously adopted. During the week men have been engaged taking the measurements for the proposed diversion of the river Irwell at Barton and on to Mem, ,at which places thp river takes a zigzag course. The measure- ments for the proposed diversion of the Briggewater Canal at Barton, so as to allow of the construction of the proposed swing bridge at the aqueduct over the Ship Canal, have already been taken.

PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS. The fortnightly meeting of the Prescot Board of Guar- dians, was held at the Union Workhouse, Whiston, on Thursday afterneon, when there were present Mr J Fish- er, (chairman), Rove T. Chambers, C W Wool!, and Dean Finegan, Messrs Spier, W Middlehurst, J Birchen, W 0 Ashton, 11. A Graves, J Ranson, Griffiths, J Ken- wright, J Ellison, and S H Hartley (clerk). untanr —The Workhouse master reported there were 434 inmates of the house this week, 447 last week, and 464 in the corresponding week last year. WORETIOTIFE ALTERATIONS.—At a meeting of the Building Committee on the 22nd ult , Mr Gandy, architect, attended' and submitted plans showing accom- modation for forty-live beds on the temale side and forty-five beds on the male side of the Workhouse. It was resolved that the further oinsideration of the plans be de- ferred until after the decision of the Board upon Mr W Middiehuret's notice of motion to rescind any resolution appropriating the clerk's Offices for the Workhouse exten- sion. The minutes were adopted.—Subsequently, according to notice given at the last meeting, Mr W Middlehurat moved that any resolution of the Board authorising premises, now occupied by • the clerk as offices, to be applied for the Workhouse extension and alteration be rescinded. He said he was perfectly confident in his own mind that the required accommodation could be provided upon the workhouse premises without at all al- tering or removing the p-esent offices or boardroom. To pull down the present offices and boardroom, and reconstruct upon their site the required -accommodation, would be ex- tremely expensive, whilst the outlay of 11,000 as he sug- gested would provide all that was required.—The Rev. Father Finegan seconded the motion.—Mr. R. A. Graves moved an. amendment that the Building Committee be asked to instruct their architect to furnish plans showing how the Board could provide accommodation without inter- fering with the offices an !boardroom, and the Rev. T. Chambers seconded the amendment, which was ultimately carried by nine votes to 2. . THE BOARD'S OFFICIALS.—The Clerk reported that the sum of £286 8a 6d bad been repaid, by the Local Govern- ment Board in respect of the salaries of the Board's poor- law imedical officers. THE RAINEILL VACANCY.--.The Clerk reported the re- ceipt' of a notice from the Local Government Board directing the election of a Guardian for the township of Rainhill, and it was decided to issue the usual notices. Cottrrry PnEcncr.-7The Clerk said be bad received a precept from the Depnty-Clerk of the Peace of the County for the sum of 8,0243 12s which had to be paid on the 30th inst.—The Rev. Dean Finegan remarked that the amount seemed very large.—The Clerk said they had no remedy in the matter. THE Ar.f.EGED -DIFFERENCE BETWEEN DOCTORS.—The Clerkatated that at the last meeting he was directed to write to Dr Hall. the Workhouse medical cfficer, in reference to the case of a man named Ward,, whom. it was stated,he had refuhed admission to the hospital after receiving an order from Dr Cooper, He had received a letter from Dr Hall, stating that he did not fecollect the .person in (*Mon, as be had to attendtso many every Morning, either in the body of the house or in the hospital. He bad, however, asaigned Thomas Warkto the body of the house, and if he had erred in doing so he would be very glad to give any further in. formation in his power. The Clerk added that Dr COoper,l ef , Widnes, who wart said to have given the mac Ward an order for the man's admission inte the hospital had not actually done so, as he (the clerk) held in his band the very certificate given by Dr. Cooper, which bad aped it " Order to the House."--The Rev. Dean Finegau remarked that this placed a new construction upon the matter;aud they did nut think there Was any blame attaching to Dr. Hall.—The Rev. T. Chambers exprerrd kiroself in a similar maaner,,and said he would inform Dr Cooper when he next saw him that it would be better if he wie ninre .careful in the future.—The- subject then drooped.' t We was the prineipal business. sl

Sir Michael Hicks-Beach has returned from Wiesbaden with his eyesight much improved. Tuesd.y, August 16th, has been fixed for the execution of the Crewe murderer, Macs Hy Bevan. The execution will take place at Knutgorcl At the Liverpool ASsizes on Wednesday, Eugene Court. ney, 29, and Ruth Courtney,4l,ware sentenced respectively to twelve month's imprisonment and five years' penal sevi. tude for keeping .a 81)am registry office for servants.

Some painters' scaffolding on the Forth Bridge gave way on Wednesday af t ern oon, and three men were hurled from a height of 140 feet. Two of them were killed, aka the third was so injured that he is not expected to recover. . . . .

Tgv Trims A GITATION.-At the tithe agitation inquiry at Denbigh on Wednesday the Commissioner stated that in order to shorten the inquiry all future evidence would be limited to the actual disturbances which had taken place. The Rector of &Mari, near Rhyl, gave his opinion that the agitation against tithes originated in "envy, hatred, and malice " atrainst the church, and upon being asked by the Commissioner to give facts and not adjectives he replied that he Mid no facts to give except the deplorable one that the tenants would net pay their tithes.—A meeting attended by several Welsh members and presided over by Mr. Stuart Rendel, M.P., was held on Wednesday night, in iho Hol- born Teen Hall. Lenclon, to protest against the methods adopted by the Government in dealing with the tithe griev- ances in Wales' and against their recent uncalled-for inter- ference with the ordinary course of justice in the caseof the pending trial of men charged with rioting,

- - • WARRINGTON RAND OF HOPE DEMONSTRATION. AND „GALA'. On Monday the annual demenstration and gala in connection with the Warrington • Band of Hope Union . took . place.. Early in the afternoon the members of the various :branches of • the Union as- sembled in front of the Town Hall, and having afterwards-paraded—some-of the\--streets•of the town proceede4lto- the ground of, the Football Club, off Wildersfobl Canseway, where the rest of the day was spent. The societies left the Park in the fol- lowing order . 200, preceded by baud; Brick-street and Friars Green, 200, with band of the Union Industrial School ; Working-men's Mission, Dank Quay, ;,200; Howley-line, 330, with band of of the South Lancashire Militia; Bewsey-road and ,ISilver-street-;Vesleyans, 200; Wycliffe Cockhedge I Miesion, 250rGplborne-street Baptists, 50; Legh- street Prinitittie Methodist, 150 ; • Bizekley-street,t 50;• .Bold-street Wesleyans, 200; St. Pauls with band, 230 ;, St.-Barnabas, 150' Sankey Bridges,loo : Emmanuel, 150, with band of the, Mersey Seamen's Mission. The route:of the procession was through I Sankey-street, Buttermarket-street, Scotland,road., Winwick-street, Tanners-lane, Bensisey-streeti Horse- kmarket-street, Bridge-street, and Wilderspool Cause- Way. It should be mentioned that the marsh ails 1 I Wer&' Messrs. • Price,' Roberts, and Ashley; Mr. T I Dale wai-chairinan of thEi'' caMinittee, and Messrs.-, Isaac „Barlow and George James, hon. secretaries. To thbss gentlemen along with the committee credit is due for .the excellent ariiingeMents.which con- duced• largely to the success of the gala. In the held during the afternoon, in addition to the juvenile members of the Band of Hope, there was a large -attendance of- adults estimated at some thousands. Performances were given by the

different band; present. Balloons were set up in the course of the afternoon, and these were a greet source of interest and pleasure, especially to the younger spectators. A good deal of interest , was likewise taken in a recitation contest which was open to four entries from each branch, viz., two ,boys and two girls. The prizes consisted of books, and were won as follovis :—First prize, girls, Ri3becca Price, nowley branch ; second, Lizzie Turner, Etnmanuel ,• first prize, boys, W. J. Price, Rowley Band of 1-tope; second, C. W. Spinks, Emmanuel. In the evening a meeting was held in the field. The Rev. G. E. Cutting presided, and there were also on the extemporised platform the Rev. F. L. Good, J. Yonge, E. -Moore, W. It. Parry, J. Llewellyn; l‘lessrs.W.Roberts, C. George, Pale, Shaw (Runcorn), and Barlow. A considerable number of persons _

gathered in front of the-platform. The CHAIRMAN, in the course of a stirring ad- dress, said he wanted those present to come over the line and do duty in connection with that great movement. ' They Could all do a great deal by their infinence, and If they did no -more than in- fluence the children they would do a great deal for the sobriety of the nekt generation. 'He had an unfaltering conviction that they were on the win- ning side, and Englishmen liked to be on the win- ning side. He knew.they would win, but if they all helped, they would win all the sooner. (Ap-

plause-.) • Tile Rev. F. 1.. Goon said he felt rather proud that on his fist anpiiiarance in Warrington on a public platform it was to advocate a cause which- he had at heart—total ab- stinenc4 connected with their Band of Hope Union. (Ap- plause.) He had strong opinions on the subject, perhaps stronger Hier many whom tht y might have heard, for he said unhesitatingly that drinking was not only an evil but a sin. (Applaurp.) He said so because for many years he had observed the misery and the ruin which hid been brought into the home of the drunkard. 'rne gaols were full of prisoners, and if they were to go round to them, and speak to the criminals, as he had frequently done, the answer they would get when they asked "What brought you here?" would be, Why, sir, it was a drop of drink." Why was it they had so many ctivainals in their laud? He unhesitatingly said it was due to the indulgence in the uee of alcohol. The workhouses were tilled, and, per hips, the ratepayers of Warrington knew that to their c rat. There- fore, when they saw so much evil around them, they must' acknowledge that that which produced it Mat be to all in- tents and purposes not only an evil in itself, but really s.n. ful. (Applause.) The Rev. J. LLEWELLYN, in the course of a brief but earnest address, remarked that it was of the greatest im- portance they should look after the children, who would be the men aud women of the future. (Applause.) The CHAIRMAN was sorry to say that his three years' association with the ministers of Warrington in that and other social movements was coining to an end. He bad en- joyed being shoulder to shoulder with the clergymen of the Church of England and with their highly esteemed Congre- gational minister, the Rev. John Yonge, in doing what he could to make Warrington a happier and a better town. lie should think of him and others when he was in Manchester, ILIA he hoped the same enthusiasm would characterise the clergy and ministers in fighting the great battle against in- temperance. (Applause.) The Rev. J. YoNCIE said he bad no doubt they would share with Itlm the deep regret be felt that their friend the chairman was so soon to be removed from them. He always thought that amongst the many advantages of the Wes- leyan Methodist system there was one very conspicuous disadvaetage, and that was in the speedy removal of their ministers. At any rate be could say so from the personal standpoint. Be had now been ha Wallington long enough to know three complete sets of Wesleyan ministers, and he had learned to esteem every one of them, and his regret had always been that almost ,as soon as be had got to knew them they had taken to themselves wings and flown away to other realms. He was sure they would wish their friend, Mr. Cutting, all possible happiness on taking his wing to a new sphere in the course of a few weeks, and he hoped his succeesor would be a man as good and true as Mr. Cut- ting had proved himself. (Applause.) There was only one man whom he would rather have seen in the chair that night than Mr. Cutting. He referred to the gentleman Vilio held the office of president of that Band of Hope Union. He did not quite know Mr. Baylor's reason for not beteg present, but be was afraid he (Mr. Naylor) had got into his head the idea that he was not a very popular man among them. If that were the case he was under a very great mistake. (Hear, hear.) They very much regretted his absence, and they hoped that if they were spared another year they should see Mr. Naylor in his proper place as chairman of that meeting. (Hear, hear.) Having wel- comed into their midst the two new allies in the cause of temperance, the Rev. F. L. Good and the Rev. J. 1). Llewellyn, Mr. Tome referred to letters which had ap- peared in "The Examiner" signed by "Clifford Dix." Many of them, he supposed, bad a very good idea who Mr. "Clifford Dix" was. Their 'knew' that "Clifford Dix " w§,l not his real natine.. (Hear, bear.) He was a man for idiom personally he had a good deal of respect. He held opinions .very much opposed to his (Mr. Yonge's) on a great many subjects. but he believed 'him to be a man of intelligence and of considerable reading. He believed hint to be an honest man, and be was sure that in the criticisms "Clifford Dix" had brought to bar on their temperance work he bad been speaking from honest motives. In one of his letters " Clifford D.x" had been criticising some of their deliverances. and said he hoped to be forgiven for the criticisms. They temperance people were not afraid of be- ing criticised, and in fact they ,rather liked it, for there were folks who would be sure to read the criticism because they liked something that was critical and censorious. They therefore readily forgave "Clifford Dix" for all he had said. "Clifford Dix" referred to the number of people in this country—he said there were millions—who bad mails it a perfectly settled question that a glass of beer was a very good tonic of the system, and that as they bad made that a settled question they intended to enjoy their grass of "X X "as often as they could get it. He (Mr. Yonge) was dirlposed to say, considering the facilities for getting glasses of " XX," that if these millions of people took advantage of all their oppartunities they would very soon cease to be moderate men. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) They might say that a glass of beer was a good tonic to the system but the most eminent medical men in the country said directly opposite, and he was there to say, so far as his own experi- ence went, that since he had given over taking; tonics of that kind he found his system was stronger than when be took the tonics. (Hear, bear.) He believed there was a great number of people who could tell them the same thing, and irany of them would give the System of total abstinence a fair, honest, and pet severing trial he thought they would come to the same conclusion he had come to himself. (Heir, hear.) "Clifford Dix " then went on to pitch into them because they always fell foul of the poor man, and he said "Why don't you pitch iato the rich people?" So far as he Yonge) was personally concerned if be bad the oppor- tunity of reaching the rich drunkards he would pitch into them, but unfortunately they hid themselves in the castle of their own homes and they could not be got at. But they could get workingmen together and they could speak to them (Hear, hear), One man was as good as another. and what they had to do was to endeavour to reach those men what- ever be their elites and whatever their standing in the social system of the country.' Bo far as he was personally en- cerned be should go on advising workingmen to become total abstainers in their own interest, and in the interest of their families at large. (Applause). it .wee . very, amusing that " Clifford Dix" hitched into the _workingmen himself although it was what he blamed them for doing. He said that "drinking is the curse and the millstone that kept the workingman down." He believed that" Clifford Dix" belonged to the noble armv.of workingmen' and be hoped they would take the, vs timbny from his lips. (Bear, hear.) In conclusion lir. Vonge moved a vote of thanks te the chairman, coupled with the expression of a sincere hope that he may have a

FRODSHAM.

- PRIMROSE LEAGUE GARDEN PARTY.—OD Tuesday after- noon the members of the Frodeham Habitation of tbe Prim- rose League were invited by Mr. James Reynolds, chief Ruling Councillor of the Habitation, to a garden par:y at Fox Hill. About 300 members accepted the invitation, and amid splendid weather a very enjoyable afternoon and even. tog was spent. BANE HOLIDaY —As usual, there were many visitors at Frodsham on Monday, from the surrounding towns and vil- lages. The chief attraction was the fir-famed OVerton Hills. For several years past there has been a flower show held at Frodsham on the August Bank Holiday, but owing to the want of interest at the meeting when the matter was considered, it was thought desirable to let the show fall through for the present. GRAND FETE AND GARDEN PARTY AT FOXHILL.-11:e the kind permission of Mr. James Reynolds, J.P,, the beautiful grounds of Foxhill, near Ftodaham, were again thrown open on Saturday afternoon and evening, although there was not such a largo number of visitors as might have been ex- pected. The entertainments in the grounds were very much similar to those previously held, with the addition of a first class concert given by several gentlemen, members of the Chester Cathedral choir. The Chester Militia Band wee ! in attendance, and enlivened the whole of the proceedings by a good selection of music. TRINITY WESLEYAN CHAPEL—The anniversary sermons ! were preached on Sueday morning and evening by the Henry Burton, M.A., of Manchester. In the afternoon, owing to the illness of Mr. John Simpson, of Dunadale. Mr. Burton emducted this service, which was more especially for the children, and delivered a short but interesting ad. dress on the manner of mdking one's life beautiful. The choir, assisted by the teachers and elder scholars, rave the hymns and anthem, "0 praise the Lord," creditably, under the leaderehip of n.lf. T. Siwt. The increase of the bank rate teaday from 2 to 3 per cent. had no effect upon the market, as the step was fulfri;r: anticipated and is only a precautionary one in anticipation , of the first drains of gold for America. Prices on the Stock 'Exchange remain almost stttionary, and brokers who are i 'obliged to be (melee spot are to be met with op some bye- straw. where a grateful share" is to be found indulging; ,in cigar or cigarette, the most peaceful model of killing the time which ha-gs so heavily on their hands. Investors just now should limit their ;transactions as much as possible; if they are unable to i 'refrain altegetber they should certainly become bearsl rather than bulls, eau this remark appliee to etock ,Ex- I Change dealings generally, as when a bull is successful Mel heavy contangu rates eats up his prefi;s, whereas in a bear account there are none of these charges to belprovided for. Tee directors of the Great Western Railway announce ' the half-yearly dividend at the rate of 4± per cent better than the corresponding half of last year, end the amount carried forward is nearly £3,00 more, The Girt Light and Coke Co. announce the half-yearly div- idend at ;berate of 12t per cent, per annum, carrying forward , sufficient to pay another 4 per cent, but it is not wise per- haps to draw too reatrattentlon by Ole immensely profitable monetoly.- The pro-dividend of 12 per cent of a bon- us of £2 on each £lO of stock hes just been declared by an- , other GUMESI and SODS Ibis thr eas Allsopps 8 per cent into the sloe& entirely, the earnings of these ocanothies are sonoshing aeounding, and when we find aid Messrs. Guirass have realized, over £637,000 during the past nine month, the barges, sum ever made in a similar period by the film, pne is aateeished that Messrs. Guineas should ever have emsired to get rid of so profitable a period. The financial editors of both the ' Daily News" and the "Telegraph" fell into an odd error in at- ; tempting to explain, this remarkable increase. Both these authorities attribute the increase to the thirsty weather. This explanation sounded very plausible, but they have overlooked the fact that the acc runts showing this profit are only made up to June is', and at that time i the hot weather had not set in. Is not -the enormous in- crease rather to be accounted for by the well-known fact that hundreds of licensed victuallers gave large orders at the time of the issee of the prospectus in the hopes of in- fluencing an allotment, and further by the tremendous ad- vertisement the phenomenal success of the companies proved for their products. What investors have to consider is whether these prole will continue. It must not be for- gotten that the raw,meterial used in brewing has been very cheap for the past nine months. Will they continue so ? ; Guinness's martini represent £850,000 per annum. They have placed £20040, to reserve. £20,000 is put aside for deprecie,ione. and £20,000 is carried farward. The magnitude of this business may be fairly realised, when it is stated that the amount carried to reserve and set aside for depreciation would suffice to pay a dividend of II on the whole of the ordinary stock- of, the Great Eastern Railway. The Bodega Company- is non flourishing according to the directors' report on the trading for the last half-year. The direc- tors do not exptain this diminutioa of business, but they do explain that they cannot cut down expenses in a corresponding degree, because they say most of the charges are of a fixed description. This seems a very extraordinary reason. But though the shareholders are not prospering, the directors are • well looked after. Among the items figuring in the- balance sheet are Managing Director, £2,13,001' "I hectors,' Fees, £600." Wiry not begin economising at this end ? I have been ,reqpested to state that the name of Mrir Lewill of 30,. Cornhill, ha been ieserted in the prospect-

tus of the Bingera. Diamond Fields Company without his knowledge or coneent and that the statement that dia- monds from the property that the C )mpanv agreed to purchase are on view at his address is without founda- tion. It is almost needless to remark that such a mis--
statement invalidates the prospectus and any person who has applied for, slimes on this representation can demand the return of his money.

The greatest excitement prevaile• among the officials of the locomotive department of the Midland Railway, as 3 ODD Men are on strike. The men have received no reply to their communication to the directors at Derby, and it is stated that the latter have determined to enforce their circular: The cause of the strike is a notice, issued recently by the 'directots stating that for the future that part of the agree-, meet effected in 1867, whereby eagiste-drivers and firemen. _not called on duty, in consequenceeef their trains being un-s expectedly stopped, have been paid as if on duty forsix dare, shall be cancelled. From midnight until five on Friday morning twelve trains were standing on the main line of, the Midland Railway be- tween New Mills and Maude. The men in charge of the• ,goods trains had deserted their train,. Expreeses.were - delayed several hours. fen trains were got to work whilst the men in charae of the en„. ines are accompanied by 'officials to direct the route. All over the country traffiet is disorganised in consequence tithe strike. Telegrams hive been receivedeby the Strike Committee at Derliy from diffnent parts of Eingland, ell denoting,that the men are firm in their resolution not to return to work. until the company's officials abandon their attempt to upset an arrangement which it is contended has =worked well for twenty years past.

TO THE ELE CTORS OF THE NORTHWICH PAR- LIAMENTARY DIVIOION OF CHESHIRE. Gawrxxsigx.—The death of your late member is peculiarly sad. He has been struck down at the crowning point of an honourable career, and at a moment when his neighbours. without distinction of class, creed, or parts*, were preparing to receive at his hands a noble gift, and arranging together how best to do him honour. It is with a sad pleasure that I recall how, in the precincts of the House of Common!, but a few short days ago, I held a long aria friendly conteren, e with him concerting measures for the future benefit of this (BAUM in which we had both so large and deep an Merest, and how cordial was the grip of his hand at pa, ting. Mr. VERDIR'S sad death imposes upon you the duty of electing a suacessw in the honourable position of member for this division. Choson a third time by the freely elected Liberal Associa- tion, I ask agates for a renewal of the trust you bestowed upon me twenty months ago, when over 5,000 men recorded their votes in my favour. At that time Iliad openly declared to you my opinion that " Ireland ought to have full power to deal with all affairs purely Irish, but that I would be no party to any enactment which would make the two minions A Irish people living in Great Britain foreigoe:s amongst us." As your repr :tentative in the House of Commons I rec owied my vote in tayour of the principle of the great measure for the better government of Ireland /aid before the Hon. e by Mr. Gladstone—that principle being declared by Mr. Gladstone to be the establishment cat a legislative assembly for Ireland em- powered to deal with purely Irish affairs. Twelve mo .ths egl, deceived by the promises of the Tory party and their alLea, to govern Ireland by the same laws as Great Britain, deceived by the false statement that the Liberal party proposed the dismemberment of the Empire, you re- jected rry offer of service. Those promises have been hamelerly broken. The Tory party and their supporters, the Dissentient Liberals, have forced upon the House of Commons and upon unwilling but helpless Ireland, a Coercion Act of fearful severity, and utterly opposed to the spirit of the British Con- stitution. I ask you to punish this breach of faith, and this you can , most effectually do by plocing me again at the head of the poll I a few days hence. I am strongly opposed. as I was last year, to the exclusion of the reps eseutatives of Ire,and from the Imperial Parliament , and I am still, as I was then, a Arm supporter of the unity of the Empire. I will do all in my power to strengthen it' and will resist with rill my might any p•oposal tending to weaken R. I cordially welcAne Mr. Gladstone's assurance that any future measure for the purchase of Irish land for the benefit of the tenants shall involve no risk of charge upon the British taxpayer. I rejoice greatly that the honest and kindly effsrt made by the Liberal Leadsra at the Round Table Conference has brought about a cordial agreement between them and Sir George Tre- velyan. All true Liberals will desire that the plan for the better goverr ment ot Ireland resulting from that agreement shall at an early date be fully and fairly placed before ills coun- try by a Government in which that true, plucky and Con- sistent Liberal etatermen will sit side by side with Mr. Glad- stone. To every man who votes for me at this election will be due a large share in the honour of bringing about that happy end. My opponent comes before you as a supporter of the Tory Government, and therefore as an upholder of exceptional coercive legislation for Ireland, as a supporter of the party of privilege and exclution, and necessarily, even in spite of him- self, an opponent of the party of progress aud freedom. I ask your support as a cmivlnced Liberal. Faggot votes must be abolished, and the principle of " one man, one vote" established. The present Pyslem of registration results in wholesale dis- franchisement, as witness the Case of Wesleyan and Primitive Method St ministers, and it must speedily be reformed. If to-morrow any man in this Division becomes a householder, he will not be entit;ed to be put on the Register until Septem- ber, 1889, and will not be able to vote until the let day of January 1890. Having seen much of the benefits of the policy cf trust in the people in Iho matter of thd control of the Liquor Trade, I am more than ever convincsd of the wisdom of that policy. Emally. gentlemen, I rs,ir for your votes as a supporter of the great Leader of the Liberal Party. Mr Gladstoi,e, sincerely believing him as Idoto be a generous, a wise, and a patriotic statesman. I remain, gentlemen, . Your faithful servant. JOHN T. BRUNNER. Wilmington Old Hall, Northwich, July 30th, 1887.

_ TO THE ELECTORS OF THE NORTHMaCH DIVISION IN THE 00UNTY OF CHESTER. OrtcrLasorx,—By the sad removal from our midst of your late friend and Member, Mr. RoairnT VEnnlls, the cause ef the Union and of Order m Parlism-tat has sustained a loss rot to be easily rep'aced. Proud as I sh,uld be to devote myself to ub ic work, as a representative of 'my native county, the knowledge of this loss, which .yon more particularly must feel, incr. aces the sense of responsibility with which I have entered upon this present contest. The ur ardmeus request which has reached me from the Conservative and Ltberal Unionist As oclations could alone en, courage me to come forward to represent the well-considered principles of p litical progress wh'eh your late Member stead- fastly meintained. I am prepared to support such equitable legislation as nsay tend ti remove the grievances of the Irish tenant farmer, sr tile the agrarian difficulties of Ireland, and improve the per- manent relations betwern that country and Great Britain. But I am determined on all occasions, and at any cost, to do my utmost to preserve the Unity of the United Blagdorn, under one supreme Parliament. I will uphold the authority of the Executive Gok ernment. which Is reep rrisible for its actions to the representative. of the People in Parliament, and I will in- sist on that rtgord for the observance of the law, which la the surest guarantee of prosperity under the democratic institu- tions which we possess. The genuine progressive policy of the present Unionist Gosr• ernment, as r hown in their proposals for relieving the Irish tenants, for reforming the English Land Laws, for abolishing the law o primogeniture, f rr provi sing the labouring c:asses with allotments, for promoting education, readj ,sting taxa, tion, and establishing Locri Government. on an effer.tive and popu`ar basis, is befors the country, and In spite of unprece dented obstruction in Parliament, over which the firmness of toe Government has ultimately prevailed, much of It has been advanced towards completion. Such measures convince me that from the Unionist Government we may confidently anti- cipate at an early date all the necessary reforms wh cii com- mend themselves to the country, without the risk of encoun- tering the unknown dangers and the certain delays which are involved ifl the acceptance of the undefined Irish policy of Mr. Gladstone. In particular I desire t r aid to the best of my ability any measures whereby the agricultural distress now unlortunately prevailing in this county may be relieved, and to encourage, sspecially by the promotion of technical education, the de- velopment of the great and special industries associated With this Division. I shall be glad to support a measure whereby marriages may be solemnised in Nonconformist places of wor ship with- out the necesshy for the presence cf the Registrar. Any other just measures which command your ssmpathy will at all times receive my best and most earnest consideration. Lam, Gentlemen, Your most obedient Servant, HIINRY GROSVENOR.
